author: AfricanFeminism
title: Eight Years in Prison for Fighting Anti-Black Racism in Tunisia: Free Saadia Mosbah!
content:
For years, Saadia Mosbah has been one of the leading voices against anti-Black racism in Tunisia. As president of the anti-racism organisation Mnemty, she has stood up for Black Tunisians and Black migrants alike. When


violence against Black migrants escalated

 after President Kais Saied’s February 2023 statement against African migrants, she became a target of online hate campaigns.


On May 6, 2024, she was arrested. On March 19, 2026, she was sentenced to eight years in prison and a heavy fine on charges of money laundering and illicit enrichment. On June 23, the Tunis Court of Appeals upheld her conviction, along with those of five Mnemty colleagues and associates. A final appeal, filed on June 29, is now before the Court of Cassation.


Human rights movements and organisations,


including Amnesty International

, have denounced the irregularities in the proceedings and the lack of evidence for the alleged offences. They have also raised the alarm over the racist treatment and violence Saadia has reportedly suffered in detention.


Saadia’s case sits within a wider pattern of repression. Since President Kais Saied seized sweeping powers in July 2021, Tunisia has slid back into authoritarian rule. Since May 2024, the month of Saadia’s arrest, the authorities have waged

a systematic crackdown on civil society

: activists prosecuted, organisations suspended, independent voices jailed. Throughout, the European Union has kept its

2023 migration deal with Tunisia

 in place, funding the country to stop people crossing to Europe and outsourcing its borders to a government that imprisons those who defend Black migrants. In this climate of repression and European complicity, Saadia’s voice and her freedom matter more than ever.


Saadia is more than a case file. Below, three activists tell their stories of the woman they know and the movement she helped build. Read them, then join the call for her immediate and unconditional release and for the convictions to be overturned. Keep fighting for those who fight for us in an anti-Black world.


 


Saadia’s Imprisonment Inseparable from Criminalisation of Black Organising and Solidarity


I first met Saadia Mosbah shortly after the 2011 Tunisian Revolution, when she was active in feminist organisations. Over the years that followed, I witnessed her unwavering commitment to the struggle for Black dignity, justice, and liberation in Tunisia. I watched her organisation, Mnemty, grow. And I watched a dream grow alongside it: the dream of a Tunisia where racism would no longer be denied, normalised, or left unpunished. 


A Tunisia with a law explicitly criminalising racial discrimination. Saadia was determined to bring together as many voices as possible around this struggle. She openly confronted a reality that many preferred to ignore: a significant part of Tunisia’s supposedly progressive and activist civil society remained silent on racism. Even within movements claiming to fight for equality and justice, Black people were too often expected to fight their battles alone.


Saadia refused that silence. She refused to make racism a secondary issue, or to soften her political demands to make others more comfortable.


But through years of persistence, political courage, and collective organising, she helped build a movement strong enough to achieve a historic victory: the adoption of Tunisia’s law against racial discrimination in 2018.


Years later, in 2023, I had the privilege and honour of working alongside Saadia to organise a march against state racism. Following the Tunisian presidency’s disgraceful statement targeting sub-Saharan African migrants, she was there, standing with us on the anti-fascist front line, organising, mobilising, supporting, and defending Black people and migrants in Tunisia. Saadia knew the risks. She understood what it meant to confront state racism in an increasingly authoritarian political climate. Yet she refused to retreat.


Today, Saadia est en prison. Her imprisonment is inseparable from the criminalisation of Black political organising, anti-racist resistance, and solidarity with migrants.


Saadia’s story is also a reminder that political victories are never irreversible.


A law can be adopted while the structures of domination it was meant to challenge remain intact. Rights written into legislation mean little when those who fought for them are deprived of their freedom.


But Saadia’s struggle is bigger than her imprisonment. It …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: IEC declares 2026 local elections free and fair as coalitions get set to run municipalities
content:
The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has declared the 2026 local government elections free and fair, with 14.9-million people having cast their ballots in an election that has left most municipal councils facing the prospect of coalition government.


The African National Congress (ANC) retained its position as the largest party nationally, securing 30.76% of the vote and 3,246 council seats. However, the result represents a significant decline in its electoral support and leaves the party needing to negotiate with other political formations in municipalities where it failed to secure an outright majority.


Announcing the results at the IEC results operations centre at Gallagher Estate on Sunday, IEC chairperson Mosotho Moepya said the elections had largely been conducted in a peaceful environment.


A total of 29.2-million voters were registered, with approximately 14.9-million participating. The national turnout was 52%, an increase of 6.1 percentage points from the 45.9% recorded in the 2021 local government elections.


The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second with 24.64% and 1,695 council seats, followed by the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) with 9.76% and 785 seats. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) received 6.22% and 588 seats, while ActionSA secured 5.67% and 313 seats.


Moepya said the commission’s declaration was informed partly by findings from the 2026 Elections Satisfaction Survey conducted by the Human Sciences Research Council. The survey found that 90% of respondents regarded the elections as having integrity, 91% considered them free and fair, and 95% were satisfied with the services provided by the IEC.


Some voting stations experienced problems with voter management devices. Photo by Mzi Velapi


However, the commission acknowledged that the electoral process had not been without challenges.


In Douglas, Northern Cape, ballot papers were destroyed before counting could take place when political party supporters allegedly stormed the voting station at a community hall. The IEC ordered a revote in Ward 3 of the Siyancuma Local Municipality, saying the affected votes could not be counted since ballot papers had been destroyed. The commission approached the Electoral Court and registered a criminal case with the police.


Chief electoral officer, Sy Mamabolo outlined the scale of the election operation, which involved approximately 188,000 staff deployed across 23,696 voting stations.


The IEC printed more than 100-million ballot papers and deployed approximately 56,000 voter management devices to support voter verification and the administration of the elections.


Mamabolo said approximately 28-million ballot papers had to be superseded following a Constitutional Court order affecting candidate lists. The order affected 181 ANC candidates in six municipalities. The commission extended the same dispensation to other parties in similar circumstances to ensure equal treatment.


The IEC also introduced a virtual results operations centre, allowing political parties and candidates remote access to selected applications and reports during the results process.


Mamabolo said the commission would assess both the successes and shortcomings of the election operation. “Operational excellence is not a destination, but it is a continuous institutional commitment,” he said.

author: Valerie Anne
title: LGBTQ+ Representation in Television Hits Devastating Lows
content:
As I’m sure you’ve noticed, LGBTQ+ representation in media is at the lowest it’s been in over a decade.

GLAAD’s latest Where We Are in TV study showed some bleak results that reflect the state of the country due to the hateful administration we live under and the wealthy conservatives who own most of the media conglomerates. Trans representation took the biggest hit, going from 33 characters to a measly SEVEN, and since three of them were on shows that were cancelled and four are from limited series, none of those seven will be returning next season. NONE. Devastating.

Twenty-five percent of LGBTQ+ characters have left our screens since last year, which brings the stats to their lowest point in over a decade. Cable television hit a 16-year low. BLEAK.

Streamers have more queer representation than cable and broadcast characters put together, but we have lost almost 100 characters from streamers as well, so even that isn’t great news. And combining streaming, cable, and broadcast, of all LGBTQ+ characters, 44% of them are characters of color, which is the lowest percentage since GLAAD’s 2017-2018 report.

Pride points out that it seems wild to imagine because some of the buzziest shows of the last few years feature queer characters: The Hunting Wives, Hazbin Hotel, Pluribus, Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry. I don’t think this show made it into the count, but we also have Sterling Point and now The Body. Queer people show up for shows that feature them, and queer people are great at telling unique stories. Alas, too many higher-ups lean on outdated Christian ideals and won’t invest in us in an effort to silence us.

This is especially wild because, while it reflects what the political times want you to believe (that queer people are outsiders, among other things), it doesn’t reflect the actual statistics. Every generation reports identifying as gayer than the last, so representation should also be at a steady increase to reflect reality, not a drastic decrease.

The actual numbers of LGBTQ+ characters on broadcast and cable shows are harrowing to look at. There are dozens of characters on any given TV show, and dozens of shows on each network, and yet the highest number among them is HBO with 15 characters. The second-highest is a big drop down, with Fox and Starz coming in with 10 characters each.

The numbers start off a little more promising for streaming, with 116 on Netflix, but then they also start dropping dramatically, with 68 on Prime Video and then again a steep drop to Hulu with 24.

I’m sure you, like I have, felt the shift even before you saw these numbers. Here at Autostraddle, we used to have to have a weekly TV roundup because there were so many queer characters on cable and broadcast shows that we couldn’t keep up with individual recaps. We used to do Pop Culture Fix twice a week to keep up with the news coming at us from all angles. And now there aren’t enough recurring characters for a weekly roundup and barely enough news for 10-15 links a week in a pop culture roundup.

It’s disheartening to see these numbers go down more and more every year when we were in such a steady incline for so long, but the fact is: We’re still here. We’re still out here writing well-rounded characters and telling our stories and watching and supporting the LGBTQ+ characters we DO still have on TV. We will not go quietly into the night. We will keep shouting and keep showing up for the queer shows doing it right until these numbers make sense again.

More queer pop culture news (that’s less depressing)

+ Phoebe Bridgers was the musical guest on this weekend’s SNL

+ Former wee lesbian (on Derry Girls) Nicola Coughlan doubles down on her pro-trans, anti-Harry Potter stance and we love her for it

+ Beanie Feldstein had nothing but lovely things to say about working with Ariana Grande on Focker-In-Law

+ Kate McKinnon and Queen Latifah are among those listed to be part of the NBC100 Live Celebration next month

+ Sarah Paulson and Holland Taylor have no plans to marry; Sarah Paulson doesn’t even like the idea of someone calling her a “wife”

+ The Hunting Wives stars Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman play fuck, U-Haul, kill in an interview, which eventually devolves into them complimenting each other’s past performances

+ Kate Berlant is going to co-host next year’s Spirit Awards

+ Rapper Young Miko has been dubbed the “Sexiest Lesbian Alive” by Curve magazine

+ Aspyn Ovard exposes fellow ex-Mormon socialites to the …

author: Cierra Bettens
title: InFocus: Is adopting permanent daylight saving time a mistake?
content:
Many of us know how we feel when it’s time to change our clocks back in the fall and forward in the spring. Sleepy – maybe even a little disoriented.

Well, on Nov. 1, citizens in six provinces and territories didn’t experience any of that because their governments scrapped the dreaded seasonal time change.

Governments had two choices: stick with standard time or daylight saving time. Standard time gives you more sun in the morning – while daylight time gives you extended sun in the evening.

Most chose to extend daylight into the evening.

But will they regret their decision?

This week on InFocus, David Prerau, one of the world’s foremost experts on daylight saving time, explains why they might.

“What happened in the U.S. anyway is nobody was much against it until it actually occurred in January 1974,” Prerau, the author of Seize the Daylight, told host Cierra Bettens. “We had an incident in 1974 where there was an energy crisis, an unexpected energy crisis. And so they put in daylight saving time year-round for a two-year period, which they thought would cover the energy crisis. And most people thought it would be good until it happened.

“Everybody saw they had to get up in the pitch dark, go to work in the pitch dark, and most people thought the worst thing was that to send their kids to school in the dark, walking on dark city streets or waiting at the bus stop on dark country roads. And so it lost popularity very quickly in the US, and I think 1974 and even though it was only a two-year plan, they got rid of it after one year because it was so unpopular.”

Anishinaabe health scholar, Dr. Amy Shawanda, said if the government wants to adopt one particular time, she supports standard time. But she added, there are impacts of changing the clocks.

“It’s not natural to our circadian rhythms,” she said. “A lot of people will feel off when the clocks change because it’s not natural to our circadian rhythms. As Indigenous Peoples, we never had to change the clocks. We just lived on the land, and so it’s not natural to who we are.

“We should really move away from the daylight saving time and not adopt it at all, because it does really go against our own circadian rhythms. It goes against our biology.”

Cierra is the host and co-producer of the of the weekly APTN News InFocus podcast. She joined APTN in 2024 as a reporter-correspondent in Winnipeg after working in campus and city news. She’s currently completing her Master of Arts in Media Studies at Concordia University in Montréal. Cierra has mixed settler and Red River Métis roots and is a member of the Manitoba Métis Federation.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Reports Say Trump Lied About Ending Aid to Israel, Funding Will Be Maintained
content:
Israeli outlets report that officials are, in fact, working to renew the funding for another five or 10 years.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump’s claim on Election Day earlier this month that the U.S. was ending its annual funding to Israel at the end of 2026 was a lie, Israeli outlets have revealed, catching Trump in a last-ditch effort to boost Republicans that was seemingly nothing more than a PR stunt.

According to reporting by Israeli outlets Times of Israel and Ynet, several Israeli and U.S. officials say that there is no such deal in place between the countries. In fact, the current agreement being hashed out is for the U.S. and Israel to enter another memorandum of understanding (MOU) when the current one ends to continue sending Israel aid.

Details have yet to be worked out, but the general outline consists of a 5- or 10-year deal to phase out the U.S.’s annual $3.8 billion in annual aid sent to Israel. One version of this, according to Ynet, is for the U.S. to maintain current funding levels — with $3.3 billion of that funding allocated under the Foreign Military Financing program — for five years, after which it would be cut off.

The goal of striking a new deal, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has openly acknowledged, is for the U.S. to wind down such financial support of Israel while further integrating the U.S. and Israel’s military sectors, with some measures to do so currently slated for passage by Congress. This would allow the countries to maintain a more secretive technology- and intelligence-sharing relationship with less public oversight.

The current MOU would continue to be funded through its end date in 2028, the reports said. Both Israeli and U.S. officials were taken aback by Trump’s announcement on November 3, reports have found, and Israeli Finance Ministry officials told members of Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, on Monday that they were not informed of the announcement nor do they know when the funding will be cut off.

Ynet and Times of Israel are right-wing outlets that often support ultranationalist movements in Israel. However, the reports add credence to suspicions that Trump was bluffing when he made his announcement. At the time, Trump openly said that he was making the announcement in order to stave off attacks from the left about Republicans’ fervor for supporting Israel, as polls portended his party’s major losses in the midterm elections.

Experts and advocates for Palestinian rights had cast doubt on the announcement. U.S. taxpayers could still be on the hook for $10 billion in outstanding military orders from Israel in coming years if Trump ends the MOU early, according to a State Department letter sent to Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) and reported by The Wall Street Journal on November 4. This is because the MOU is structured so that Israel orders U.S. weapons and equipment in advance, and is later provided the money by the U.S. to pay for it.

“It’s not plausible there will be a total cut-off starting January 1,” said Josh Paul, a former State Department official working on foreign arms procurement, to The Intercept shortly after Trump’s initial announcement. “My guess is that he was speaking off the cuff with the next 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel in mind, but did so in a way that is at best inaccurate or imprecise.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $28,000 in the next 72 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Gaurav Kumar
title: How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline
content:
This article

How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On Nov. 7, the eve of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, the leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, including founder Abhijeet Dipke, were not at home. They were marching in Kochi, a port city in the southern state of Kerala, nearly 1,300 miles from Delhi. 


The march echoed the two demands the movement had been shouting in Delhi’s streets since the first week of October: Scrap the nationwide recheck of voter rolls that began in June 2025, and sack the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. 


The Cockroach movement came into being in May of this year and won its first victory in July, pushing India’s education minister out of office over a leaked national medical entrance exam. The open question then was whether

a movement with no one leader and no office

 would still be around after winning its first fight. It is, and while it still has no office, it has picked a much bigger fight. Not an exam this time, but the vote itself.


The Election Commission, which runs India’s elections, is rechecking every one of India’s nearly one billion voters. In the name of clearing the rolls of the dead, the duplicated, people who have moved and what its

June 2025 order

 called “foreign illegal immigrants,” it has

purged more than 130 million

 voters. In Delhi alone, the cleanup has knocked 4.76 million people, nearly a third of the city’s electorate, off the voter list. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, strongly backs the recheck, saying that it’s necessary to strike undocumented migrants from neighboring Bangladesh, particularly Muslims, who have slipped onto the rolls. Amit Shah, Modi’s home minister and most powerful lieutenant, has defended the recheck as a way to “detect, delete, deport” what he calls infiltrators.

But critics charge

 that the rolls are being manipulated to benefit the BJP. They say the recheck shifts the burden of proof onto voters, and that the people least likely to have the required documents are the ones being dropped. 


Human Rights Watch found

 that the purge has disproportionately affected women, the poor and Muslims; in one area of West Bengal that is nine percent Muslim, more than 92 percent of those deleted were Muslim.

Opposition leaders

 have called the recheck a backdoor version of the National Register of Citizens, a citizenship list the BJP promised in 2019 to extend across India.


Presiding over it all is Kumar, whose commission both referees India’s elections and runs the recheck. He was handpicked by Modi in February 2025 under a new law giving Modi more power over the selection, in a decision announced late at night over the written dissent of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi.


In late September, the national daily

The Indian Express


reported

 that two of the election commission’s three members, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had objected on record at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders tied to the recheck that they say were issued in the commission’s name without their knowledge. (In an official statement, the commission maintained that all of its decisions on the recheck were unanimous.) 


Previous Coverage


What India’s Cockroach Party won — and what’s next


The Cockroach movement, which had been pressuring the government since July over broken promises, responded by calling Kumar the biggest threat to India’s democracy and giving him 48 hours to resign.


When Kumar ignored the movement’s deadline, it took to the streets of Delhi and other cities on Oct. 2, the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who led India’s nonviolent struggle for independence.


Unlike most Indian police forces, Delhi’s police do not answer to the city’s elected government but to the federal Home Ministry, run by Shah. It answered the protests the way it did in July, only harder. On Oct. 10 police detained more than 2,000 people in Delhi, opposition leaders and journalists among them, while about 600 were detained in Mumbai, India’s financial capital, and mobile internet went dark in the heart of Delhi.


Two days later

, Jantar Mantar — a square just a short walk from Parliament that has been Delhi’s main protest site for decades and was occupied by the movement for five weeks this summer — was …

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Various Molson, Coors beer brands under nationwide recall
content:
A national food recall for several brands of beer due to “metal contamination” does not affect products on Nunavut’s beer and wine store shelves, the Finance Department announced Friday.


The recall was first announced Nov. 9 due to the possible presence of small pieces of metal inside the affected products.


Various beers produced by Molson Coors Beverage Co. are affected, including Coors Light, Molson Canadian and Blue Moon Belgian-Style Wheat Ale.


The only non-alcoholic beverages on the list are six- and 24-packs of Non-Alcoholic Blue Moon Belgian-Style Wheat Ale.


The exact items, including packaging and UPC codes,

can be found

 on the Canadian Health Inspection Agency website.


None of the alcoholic beverages listed are in the Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission’s current inventory, according to the announcement from the Finance Department.


Non-alcoholic beers are available in grocery stores. Consumers are urged not to sell, distribute or drink products included on the list.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

However, the policy faced legal challenges from three transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons, including one transgender woman and two transgender men. Their attorneys argued that the new restrictions would force the end of treatments that the Bureau of Prisons had provided to people with gender dysphoria since 1992.

The policy could affect nearly 1,000 incarcerated people in federal custody. The lawsuit raises questions about whether the government can discontinue established medical treatments for incarcerated people and what constitutional protections apply to people in its custody.

A lower federal court blocked the administration from enforcing the policy. The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause that ruling and allow the restrictions to take effect while the case continued. On October 21, the Supreme Court rejected the emergency request in an unsigned order. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas stated that they would have granted the request. The decision leaves the lower court’s order in place, preventing the administration from immediately enforcing the restrictions.

However, the Supreme Court’s decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine whether the administration’s policy is constitutional. The legal challenge will continue in the lower courts.

The case highlights the challenges transgender people face when seeking health care in settings where the government controls their medical decisions. Incarcerated people depend on prison authorities for access to doctors, medication, and other necessary services so when a policy restricts particular treatment, people in custody may have limited options for obtaining care independently.

Although the ruling does not end the case, it prevents the Trump administration from immediately implementing the restrictions while the legal proceedings continue. The outcome of the lawsuit will have important consequences for transgender people in federal prisons if the restrictions are placed and as the case moves forward, it shows the importance of questioning how government policies affect vulnerable populations and how government decisions apply to people whose freedom and access to healthcare are already limited.

author: kelsie kilawna
title: The taste we’ve been missing
content:
Graphic by Lauren Marchand


The clanking of pots and pans and the ringing of laughter while moving around the kitchen were always calming sounds to me growing up. 


The most important lessons I’ve learned about food came as I stood at the hips of my grandmothers, watching them peel potatoes and listening to their stories.


I am a culinary storyteller of syilx foodways. In my work at

Smoke on the Plateau

, I teach through food. I share stories about my syilx/Okanagan homelands through a fully embodied experience bringing together taste, sight, smell and sound. My research has been lifelong and has taken place in kitchens, in berry patches, and while waiting for salmon and deer to return so I could help prepare it for the people. 


There is a beauty to this way of knowing and living, because it is what taught me to be slow and patient with the offerings of our land.


The work I do honours the relationships that collapse time and place into story. It is a way of ensuring we never forget the importance of our Four Food Chiefs system. In essence, this is a reaffirmation of our governance system. 


Now, today when you enter the Okanagan Valley, you see another food story being told. A palate cleanser for the gentrification of our foodways.


What’s missing from culinary discussions


A rising culinary hotspot, the Okanagan has dressed itself in words like “local,” “seasonal,” “farm-to-table.” While wine glasses clink and tasting notes are murmured, words like “terroir” roll off the tongue as a somewhat promise to its authenticity.

It is a beautiful and comfortable story.


Terroir is a French term embraced by the culinary industry to speak to “the taste of place.” The concept itself describes how the climate and land conditions of an area affect the flavour profile of local food crops. 


In the Okanagan this is popularized through the wine industry. It’s often the terroir of a wine that is showcased through wine tastings. It speaks to the soil, weather, topography and tradition that shape what consumers taste. 


“Local” has now become a premium label, “farm-to-table” has become marketing copy, and “terroir” has become a way to charge more for the same soil that syilx Peoples have been tending since the time of our Creation, without acknowledging who did the tending, or what was given back in return.


This is gentrification. 


Not just through the extractive wine industry, but it’s become the gentrification of taste itself. 


When terroir is extracted from its French roots and planted in the Okanagan, it lands on soil that is already alive with syilx knowledge and responsibility. 


First Foods Board, Smoke on the Plateau Catering, An assortment of homesmoked deer and elk sausages, cedar smoked candied salmon, accompanied by homemade xusem raspberry compote, and siya jam. Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)


As a syilx culinary storyteller, I am responsible for reminding people of this, that our foodways should not be minimized for the sake of an entertaining evening.


Our foodways have and always will be prayed over. Ceremonies of health, and gratitude are held for all our homelands offer us. Young people go through their Coming of Age ceremony learning to pray for the health of our waterways. All of this is the missing spirit of the term terroir.


So I’ve been working to name what’s missing. One word, something that can hold the weight of kinship, of reciprocity, of generations coiled into one. Something that reminds us we are part of the land, not separate from it.


So I call it by it’s name, tmixʷ.


tmixʷ is the nsyilxcen word for life-force, the aliveness of every being that makes a place what it is, it speaks far beyond just soil and climate. Rather it speaks to the kinships between all of it, our reciprocity, and our syilx/Okanagan obligation to give back, so that what you take can live again.


The syilx/Okanagan understanding of place is through tmxʷulaxʷ, which speaks to the life-force-place. It is a dynamic, regenerative relationship between all beings, which the culinary industry’s shallow “local” label cannot contain.


The Okanagan culinary industry wants you to taste place, so what they’re selling is terroir, but what its missing is tmixʷ.


What tmixʷ tastes like


Let me tell you a story about xusem (soapberries).


There’s a small spot in the Okanagan mountains that has the sweetest soapberries my family has ever tasted. 


The oldest person in my family shared that those berries are …

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

author: Unknown
title: “Gen Z Regulates” : A New Wave of Unrest in Germany?
content:
For months, unrest has been spreading across Europe. In

Spain

, a movement against evictions and gentrification culminated on November 11 in a countrywide general strike. In

France

, student revolt set off the most intense street confrontations since the

Yellow Vest movement

. Albania has seen wave upon wave of clashes since last February. On Halloween, the European youth protests finally reached Germany.


Under the motto

“Gen Z regelt”

 (“Gen Z regulates”), tens of thousands took to the streets of nearly 40 German cities on October 31. While a large-scale uprising like the

one

 in France remains unlikely, the first cracks in the pacification of society are starting to show. In this report, two anarchists describe their experiences in two different demonstrations and discuss the potential of the events.


More demonstrations on the same theme are scheduled for

November 20

.


A stylish banner in front of the “Gen Z Regelt” protest in Göttingen. What would Goethe have said?


Germany in Crisis


The demonstration on October 31 took place in a general context of crisis. In Germany, as elsewhere around the globe, inflation has run rampant over the last six years, driven by the pandemic, Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and the consequent loss of cheap natural gas from Russia, and, most recently, the US-Iran war.


Another growing influence on the economy is the climate catastrophe. It is

estimated

 that Germany will lose around 30 billion euros a year as a consequence of its impact. In one week, a heatwave at the end of June

killed

 close to 10,000 people. Unlike countries that have long-term experience with temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius, only 10% of homes in Germany have air conditioning; with the exception of intensive care units and operating rooms, most hospitals and nursing homes don’t have it, so people who experienced heat stroke were treated in overheated rooms. Senior citizens and those with preexisting health problems were especially hard hit: in at least one nursing home, temperatures

reached

 up to 50 degrees Celsius.


A protester in the German city of Essen asks to stop some of the impacts of climate change.


Who dies as a consequence of climate change is determined mostly by class. Germany also faces a housing crisis—

something like 53% of people live in rented homes

—and the cheapest flats are generally located right beneath the roofs of buildings several stories high. These buildings were built to keep heat in, so during heat waves, temperatures in the flats at night often stayed above the outside temperatures at same time.


On top of this, the government comprised of the neoliberal left (SPD) and Christian conservative (CDU/CSU) parties has introduced an unpopular austerity program in order to push through a massive increase in military spending, which started after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It would take another article to list all the financial cuts involved. Workers and middle-class people will have many billions less in “social benefits”—in other words, they get less back from the work and resources that the state and capitalists take from them.


Some 12% of all jobs in Germany are

directly in state institutions

, in addition to fully state-owned companies and other organizations connected to the state, like the public health insurance agencies and public media companies. Many of these have stop hiring because of the financial situation. At the same time, German economic growth is stagnating. Consequently, “Gen Z” career entrants confront a context in which companies are trying to figure out how to use artificial intelligence to replace them amid an employment market that is already much worse than previous generations faced. This is undermining the last vestiges of a social contract between companies and the state on one side and segments of the youth on the other.


Study, get degree, and you can have a middle-class life? Not anymore.


Finally, some international fashions trends like ski glasses are reaching German youth.


Unemployment is rising among university and college graduates. The social situation isn’t as catastrophic as it has become in other countries, but by contrast with many other countries, people in Germany do not have much experience helping each other directly. German society has focused on the state as the only thinkable source of support when people lose their jobs or experience other setbacks.


As a result, anger has spread …

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: a14 – What’s fermenting underground – Jazz Dance with today’s zine scene
content:
Our collective can barely process all the correspondence coming our way. The least of which comes with scrappy limited edition zines. We endeavor to highlight them here when we can. Thankfully we have found a bright and wise ally who, when not tending to the garden warmly sits and reads deeply and widely freaky shit on paper. Maybe you will find a new life of reading zines, reviewing or even making them to thicken the plot we’re in.

Ear of Corn #66 24 pages – $2 foodfortunata@hotmail.com

It’s really endearing that even after 18 years, Ear of Corn still uses pasteup for the design, even as it’s moved to glossy paper. You can see on every page that Ear of Corn is still assembled old school and copied like we all used to do at Kinkos with glue sticks. The glue had a mild starchy taste, slightly sweet with a bitter finish; not unlike bad cheese pizza.

I have this conspiracy theory about this zine. I usually write reviews in batches, and I’ll often have multiple issues of Ear of Corn on my desk at a time. But I’ve never had any sequentially numbered issues. I’ve begun to suspect issues are not numbered non-sequentially or perhaps they are sequential, but aren’t printed in that order. Their practice of reviewing old and new releases side by side makes it impossible to know for sure; but they’re definitely up to something other than eating the glue.

Out From The Void #8 $5 – 70 pages outfromthevoid@yahoo.com

This issue goes places Out From The Void hasn’t gone before. The new topics are mostly adjacent to the core topic: the missing. So it’s the CAHOOTS program, police records requests, suicide, and police killings. But on page 51 begins a 6 page essay about Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It’s sober, historical and philosophical without trumpeting statistics.

In the middle of Issue #8 is a photo essay reprinted from the zine Here’s What I’ve Hidden Under My Tongue. Writer DJT was visiting an abandoned and mostly collapsed mental institution. In the introduction Brenton Gicker comments that he didn’t write any of the stories in this issue. I appreciate that Gicker puts his mission ahead of his ego to spread awareness of these topics but I do miss his voice as a writer. But until next time, we get more tales of the missing, the lost and the found.

The story of James B. Hunt and Fluke goes back to issue #16 of the infamous Fluke fanzine in 2018. Kudos if you kept that issue, it’s now a fine collectible. Even Maximum RockNRoll said so. They saw the future, perhaps even more clearly than I did. Gina Murrell always had a sixth sense for such things. But if you wake up feeling a bit goth, have a soft spot for monsters, or just like dead stuff, NXOEED might be for you.

If you don’t recognize his art that tells me you don’t skate bruh. His art appears on show flyers, album covers, websites, rad stickers and other greasy places. But among all that ephemera this issue is special. Usually Mr. Hunt lets the ink speak for him, but this time we actually get a few precious pages of text; our first sense of the man himself. He’s a geezer, like me, trying to do punk rock things, but to also go to bed on time. I feel that in my soul.

$20 – 192 pages inequitypress@hotmail.com

It’s hard to say that many poets are famous today. But as poets go, some of those published in Big Hammer are highfalutin people now like David Cope, Donald Lev, Chris Stroffolino, Ken Greenley, and Enid Dame (RIP). Others, like Michael Pingarron, are still writing for Big Hammer. They’ve found their layer of strata, and one would hope some sense of belonging.

The first issue of Big Hammer rolled off the press in 1988. That was 38 years ago, kids. Statistically most of you reading this weren’t even born yet. That zine was way underground, like the Lincoln Tunnel; like the FDR Train Car in the pitch blackness of Track 61 marooned below Grand Central since 1945. But Dave Roskos is still out there in the tunnels, in the darkness, still editing and publishing Big Hammer. He’s doing it his own way, and accountable to no one. Doesn’t it sound grand?

Zine content from the eighties makes more sense in the context of its contemporary punk 7-inches” like “Too scared to be queer,” “Be a Fag,” and “Forbidden Love.” So I queued up the Homocore Hit parade cassette, and pondered its place in history. Homocore ran for just 7 issues between 1988 and 1991. If you didn’t catch my drift, it tapped into two communities which still remain the core of the underground today: queers and …

author: Unknown
title: “How Has Serving Impacted You?” : Veterans of the US Military in Their Own Words
content:
What is it like to serve in the United States military? If only it were possible for those who are considering enlisting to learn the unvarnished truth. In 2019, a viral

tweet

 from the official US Army twitter account unexpectedly drew over 11,000 candid replies in the course of 48 hours. These responses offer a rare window into the real experiences of servicemembers and veterans. We present a selection of them here for the benefit of anyone who is thinking about joining the military.


This is a document of an

earlier era

 of social media, captured here before it

vanishes

. You can obtain a book collecting the first twenty-four hours of responses

here

.


Just before Memorial Day in 2019, the United States Army made a strategic blunder almost on par with invading Vietnam. They posted this inquiry on their official Twitter account:


In response, veterans and their family and friends posted thousands upon thousands of tweets recounting broken promises and broken people. They described cancer, PTSD, domestic abuse, unpaid college and housing loans, Gulf War syndrome, insomnia, sexual abuse, poverty, Agent Orange, racism, nightmare disorder, unemployment, burying loved ones, misogyny, orphaned children, burn pit syndrome, homelessness, debilitating injuries, divorce, alcoholism, disappearances, a Veterans Affairs department that was unwilling or unable to help, and suicide, suicide, suicide.


The United States military is one of the largest concentrations of power in the world. With

tens of thousands

 of missiles,

millions

 of firearms, and over

5000

 nuclear weapons—about 40% of all the nuclear weapons in the world—the US military can hold the entire world hostage.


The US military is also the largest employer in the United States,

employing

 almost 2,900,000 workers—roughly 17 out of every 2000 people. If we add private military contractors like Blackwater (250,000 workers), the employees of non-combat support companies like Halliburton who build military infrastructure, provide food, and the like (150,000-250,000), US-based war manufacturers like Lockheed Martin and Boeing (1,500,000), and

veterans

 who receive disability or pension payments (2,000,000), we find that roughly 1 out of every 50 Americans is economically dependent on US militarism.


As in all industries, without this workforce, the military would grind to a halt. It especially depends on regular transfusions of young blood—young people sold stories about adventure, duty, and upward mobility.


If we were to ask new recruits why they joined, we’d

likely

 hear a mix of narratives about gaining strength, seeing the world, paying for college, serving God and country, learning life skills, continuing a family tradition, escaping poverty or an unsafe home, obtaining housing, having fun, and protecting loved ones. Most people join the military because they think it will benefit them or because they believe they are serving a higher calling.


Some recruits get to live out their dreams. Some leave instability, danger, or deprivation for a more structured and economically stable life; some even gain a sense of belonging. If they’re lucky, they serve their time without incident, then move on to free college tuition, a no-down-payment housing loan, health insurance, and a free meal at Golden Corral once a year.


But thousands of veterans’ dreams become nightmares. The promises of recruiters, family members, and Hollywood movies offer a gamble at best—a roll of the dice that

frequently

 ends with being harmed physically, psychologically, and sexually. Military service can lead to

substance abuse

,

homelessness

, and

suicide

. It can also end in unspeakable acts of violence against others, whether those be the declared enemies of the United States, noncombatants, or veterans’ own loved ones.


It is striking how many of these responses speak of being hoodwinked out of college, housing loans, and medical care—how many describe the pain of family members lost to PTSD, alcoholism, or suicide after witnessing or committing atrocities.


American media bombards us with war propaganda. Almost every video game spreads the myth that combat makes us stronger: more powerful weapons, tougher armor, a bigger health bar, greater fortunes. Hollywood promises that the hero can weather any fight—or, if he can’t, his death will be meaningful and glorious.


Statistically speaking, the more we are exposed to combat, the more likely we are to be …

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

author: anred
title: Triple lesbicidio de Barracas: llega el veredicto y movilizan a Tribunales para exigir que se reconozca el crimen de odio
content:
Foto: Ariel Gutraich / Archivo Agencia Presentes.


A más de dos años del ataque incendiario en una habitación de una pensión de Barracas, este miércoles 18 de noviembre se conocerá el veredicto del juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas. La Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más convoca a concentrarse desde las 9 frente al Palacio de Tribunales para exigir que la sentencia contra Justo Fernando Barrientos reconozca el ataque como un crimen de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género.

La fiscalía y las querellas solicitaron prisión perpetua, mientras que la defensa pidió la absolución del acusado y, subsidiariamente, que se descarten los agravantes. El proceso busca establecer la responsabilidad penal por el ataque que terminó con la vida de Andrea Amarante, Pamela Cobbas y Roxana Figueroa y dejó gravemente herida a Sofía Castro Riglos.

 Por ANRed.


Este miércoles 18 de noviembre se conocerá el veredicto del juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas.

La Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más convoca a concentrarse desde las 9 frente al Palacio de Tribunales para exigir que la sentencia contra Justo Fernando Barrientos reconozca el ataque como un crimen de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género

. La fiscalía y las querellas solicitaron prisión perpetua, mientras que la defensa pidió la absolución del acusado.


La audiencia ante el Tribunal Oral en lo Criminal y Correccional N° 5 comenzará a las 9:30 con las respuestas de las acusaciones a los planteos de la defensa y las últimas palabras del imputado. La lectura del veredicto está prevista para las 11.

La convocatoria invita a organizaciones, activistas y a toda la comunidad a acompañar la jornada y reclamar justicia por Andrea Amarante, Pamela Cobbas y Roxana Figueroa, además de justicia y reparación para Sofía Castro Riglos, única sobreviviente del ataque

.


Imagen: archivo Perycia.


El hecho ocurrió durante la madrugada del 6 de mayo de 2024, en una habitación de una pensión ubicada en la calle Olavarría al 1600, en el barrio porteño de Barracas. Allí vivían las cuatro mujeres lesbianas, que compartían un espacio habitacional en un contexto de precariedad económica y habitacional. Según la acusación, Barrientos, vecino del lugar que había protagonizado episodios previos de hostigamiento y amenazas, arrojó un artefacto incendiario contra la habitación. Como consecuencia del ataque, Andrea, Pamela y Roxana murieron, mientras que Sofía sobrevivió con graves secuelas.


Durante el juicio oral, que comenzó el 18 de mayo de este año, las querellas y la fiscalía sostuvieron que el ataque estuvo motivado por el odio hacia la orientación sexual de las víctimas. Los testimonios de vecinas y allegadas reconstruyeron las situaciones de hostigamiento que atravesaban las mujeres, mientras que las pericias de bomberos y especialistas apuntaron a que el incendio fue intencional.

Las acusaciones solicitaron prisión perpetua y reclamaron que se contemplen los agravantes de odio por orientación sexual y de género, junto con los restantes agravantes penales

.


Imagen: archivo Enfant Terrible.


Una de las particularidades del proceso fue la participación de

una querella colectiva impulsada por la Federación Argentina LGBT (FALGBT+)

, que representa a la comunidad en el juicio. Su intervención constituye un antecedente inédito en un debate judicial de estas características y fue posible luego de que la Cámara de Casación habilitara su incorporación, tras anteriores rechazos durante la etapa de instrucción.


Por su parte, la defensa de Barrientos, encabezada por

Ricardo Antonio Richiello

, pidió la absolución por el beneficio de la duda y cuestionó las pruebas testimoniales y periciales presentadas durante el debate. De manera subsidiaria, solicitó que se descarte la aplicación de los agravantes de odio y violencia de género y que, en caso de una condena, se considere una figura penal menos grave. También cuestionó la constitucionalidad de la prisión perpetua y las medidas de reparación económica reclamadas para Sofía.


Imagen: Agencia Presentes.


Desde la Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más remarcaron que el reclamo excede la determinación de la responsabilidad penal del acusado: «Exigimos que la causa se nombre como lesbicidio y que la sentencia contemple el agravante de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género, además de la violencia de género».

author: Administrador
title: Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen. Teil 6: GESCHENKE
content:
Musik: „Es que yo te quiero a ti“, Kevin Kaarl Bilder, Schnitt und Produktion: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas

Ich glaube, es war im Juli, als Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés den Beginn der ersten Etappe der „Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko“ ankündigte. Ich glaube, er sagte damals in etwa, dass die suchenden Mütter wie unsere Mamas seien. Damit nahm das Problem seinen Anfang, wie es so schön heißt.

Denn wir alle aus der Truppe dachten: „Oha, das sind unsere Mamas, und wir werden sie besuchen. Auf keinen Fall können wir da ankommen und einfach sagen: ‚Bin da, Chefin, was gibt’s zu essen?‘“. Nein, wenn wir so ankommen, bekommen wir nur die Sandale, einen Klaps oder einen fiesen Kniff (denn nette gibt es ja auch) zu spüren. Denn die oder der Freund:in – na ja, das geht vorbei, dann ist es wieder gut und fertig. Aber wenn die Mamas sauer werden, lieber Gott im Himmel, da gibt’s kein Entkommen.

„Wir sollten ein Geschenk mitnehmen“, sagte einer. „Ja“, antwortete eine Insurgenta (*), „so wie wir Mutter Erde unsere ehrliche Arbeit schenken.“ Der Capitán meinte: „Ja, als vorbeugendes Geschenk. Also noch bevor die Standpauke losgeht, hast du das Geschenk schon parat, und wenn der Sturm losbricht, holst du das Geschenk raus, lächelst und machst ein Gesicht wie: ‚Mama, ich bin‘s, der kleine Marcos, und ich werde keinen Unfug anstellen.‘“

„Das glaubt dir doch kein Mensch“, mischt sich SubMoy ein und fügt hinzu: „Außerdem steht in allen sozialen Netzwerken, dass du keine Manieren, also keine Mutter hast.“

Die Diskussion ging weiter und alle einigten sich, dass es ein Geschenk geben solle. Aber dann gab es viel Wirbel darum, welches Geschenk das sein sollte. Vielleicht Blumen. „Nein, Compa, die sind schon verwelkt, wenn du in den Bus steigst.“ „Ein Gedicht“, schlägt eine andere Insurgenta vor. Darauf SubMoy: „Die Pueblos werden schon Briefe, Gedichte und Lieder schicken. Obwohl ich nicht weiß, ob die suchenden Mütter Hip-Hop und Rap und sowas mögen.“

Die Diskussion ging weiter. Und zog sich immer weiter hin. Und dann wurde es noch schlimmer, als ein Insurgente (**) vorschlug: „Schenken wir ihnen doch ein Andenken.“

Da kam es zum Tumult. Alle redeten durcheinander: Was für ein Andenken denn, wo sollen sie das hinstellen, das ist keine gute Idee, doch, ist es, denn die Erinnerung ist das Wichtigste, deshalb sind sie ja Sucherinnen. Wenn sie keine Erinnerung hätten, würden sie aufgeben, in Ohnmacht fallen.

Da sagten die Frauen – mit dieser schlechten Angewohnheit, die Frauen haben, Diskussionen zu beenden, gerade wenn es richtig spannend wird: Stickereien und Puppen. „Damit sie wissen und sich daran erinnern, dass sie hier Familien haben.“

Die Insurgentes, angeführt vom Capitán, widersprachen und argumentierten, dass Puppen und Stickereien was für kleine Mädchen seien, dass die suchenden Mütter doch schon groß seien, dass sie gar keine Zeit für Spielereien hätten, und dann noch Stickereien, dass das einfach nicht zu glauben wäre. Die Insurgentas wurden wütend und entgegneten, dass es nichts bringe, so zu denken, weil es sich um Erinnerungen handele, nicht um Spielzeug oder Schmuck.

Und die Diskussion geht weiter, aber jetzt ist alles durcheinander, weil dem Insurgente, der für die Verpflegung zuständig war, die Bohnen angebrannt waren – und das nur, weil er sich in das Gerede um das Geschenk eingemischt hatte. Und einen Moment lang machen Frauen und Männer gemeinsame Front, denn eine Sache ist, sozusagen, der Schlagabtausch, und eine andere sind die angebrannten Bohnen. Aber dann trösteten sich alle mit Tostadas und Reis nach vietnamesischer Art. Doch es war nur ein Waffenstillstand, so unbeständig wie das Temperament von Trump. Und so ging es, nachdem sie das Geschirr gespült und die Hunde und Kätzchen gefüttert hatten, weiter.

Da kam SubMoy hinzu: „Was streitet ihr denn so?“ Alle fingen quasi an, das Problem darzulegen. „Jetzt hört aber auf damit“, rief SubMoy. Es wurde ganz still. Die Männer hofften, dass sich der Sub auf die Solidarität unter Männern besinnen würde. Und die Frauen hofften auf sein gutes Urteilsvermögen.

SubMoy zündete sich eine Zigarette an und dachte nach. Nach einer Weile sagte er: „Macht eine Liste mit dem, was wir besorgen müssen.“

Die Insurgentas applaudierten. Die Insurgentes verzogen das Gesicht, sagten aber nichts, denn die Strafe bestand darin, die angebrannten Bohnen zu essen.

Also machten sich alle Insurgentes, gleich welcher Position, daran, Geschenke zu basteln. In aller Eile, denn bis …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado y llamado Internacional del Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC
content:
Como Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC hacemos un llamado de solidaridad para enfrentar a la ofensiva ecocida de la multinacional fascista $hilena Celulosa CMPC, comandada por los Matte, en el territorio ancestral Guaraní M’Byá y lafken Guaíba, Barra do Ribeiro, sur de Bra$il.

El pasado miércoles 11 de noviembre se realizó una manifestación y marcha en el centro de Porto Alegre, donde se reunieron más de 300 personas para exigir la retirada total de dicha empresa y su nefasto «Projeto Natureza».

El «Projeto Natureza» es una planta procesadora de celulosa que pretende instalarse a las orillas del Rio Guaíba, en el fundo Barba Negra y en la Ponta da Formiga, territorio sagrado Guaraní M’byá. Su objetivo es duplicar la capacidad de producción total de celulosa de la CMPC. Hoy, cuentan con 44 plantas de procesamiento de celulosa en el continente, 3 de ellas en territorio $hileno, sumado a la planta que ya está instalada a las orillas del Guaíba en el municipio del mismo nombre. CMPC tiene la capacidad de producir 4,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Con el Projeto Natureza, su capacidad de producción podría llegar a 7,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Las consecuencias a largo plazo son difíciles de dimensionar, pero es sabido que el proyecto incluye el dragado del Guaíba, deforestación del bosque nativo, cambios en las leyes de protección ambiental, contaminación del agua y, sin dudas, la expansión masiva de plantaciones de eucalipto en Brasil, Uruguay y Argentina.

Al finalizar la marcha se realizó una acción directa coordinada en contra de la FEPAM, órgano del gobierno que otorga los permisos ambientales y de instalación a la CMPC. Manifestantes hicieron okupación de la institución, rayaron las paredes exigiendo «FUERA CMPC» y denunciando el actuar corrupto de la FEPAM, quienes ignoran por completo decenas de informes y cuestionamientos técnicos de diversas áreas sobre el impacto real de este proyecto en el territorio. Marcaron las paredes pulcras de ese actual antro de mafiosos que solo sirve como pantalla, ya que sin escrúpulos aprueban cualquier proyecto extractivista que se les ponga en frente.

El río Guaíba es parte medular de la vida en la ciudad de Porto Alegre y la región metropolitana. Es el horizonte con el que nos relacionamos cada día y gran parte del agua potable proviene de las aguas tratadas de este rio. Cuando protestamos contra la CMPC necesitamos que se entienda que esta empresa pretende derramar más desechos en el rio que toda la ciudad en su conjunto. Es un proyecto que básicamente contaminará el agua de consumo público de la región.

El actual gobierno de Lula, que basó su propaganda en ser una “alternativa al fascismo”, apoya y fomenta abiertamente el proyecto de la Familia Matte y la CMPC, que además de usurpar sistemáticamente territorio mapuche, apoyaron la dictadura de Pinochet y promovieron la Masacre de Laja en la que 19 trabajadores de la CMPC fueron fusilados por militares chilenos. El presidente Lula concedió a la CMPC una terminal portuaria de exportación en el puerto de Río Grande, en este puerto la empresa está asociada a Ultramar, empresa de la família Von Appen con infame trayectoria nazi.

Esta concesión transforma al rio Guaíba y a la Laguna dos Patos en hidrobia de madera y celulosa, impactando drásticamente la naturaleza y la pesca artesanal. Todo esto sin respetar y seguir los protocolos Guaraní y menos la convención 169 de la OIT que se supone consulta de manera previa, libre e informada a las comunidades indígenas afectadas. Esta maliciosa colaboración entre el gobierno y la CMPC se logra a través de la entrega de millones de pesos a algunas autoridades ancestrales para otorgar el visto bueno al gobierno, dividiendo a las comunidades y generando rupturas entre ellas.

Sobre la familia Matte es importante hacer memoria de que no es solo dueña de la celulosa CMPC, sino que también es dueña de Colbún, responsable por secar el Lago Chapo en la Región de Los Lagos en $hile, y de la Forestal Mininco, vieja empresa forestal conocida robar tierra mapuche, devastar bosque nativo, secar la tierra y por el asesinato de Alex Lemún de 17 años y de Pablo Marchant de 25, ambos asesinados en contexto de recuperación territorial y defensa de la tierra.

También, en 2021 se hizo famoso Fernando Puga Matte, uno de los integrantes de dicha familia, dueño del condominio de lujo Riñimapu donde trabajaban los «jardineros» que asesinaron a Emilia Milen, la Bau …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Gaza versus Ucrania: la diferencia entre un genocidio y una guerra, en cifras
content:
Hay números que no necesitan adjetivos. Ponemos una al lado de la otra las cifras de Gaza y de Ucrania, las de las fuentes oficiales y las de los organismos internacionales, y dejamos que hablen. Todas son terribles, porque cualquier guerra es una tragedia humana. Pero no todas las muertes responden a la misma lógica.


Los niños, el primer termómetro.


En Ucrania, desde febrero de 2022, la ONU (OHCHR) ha verificado 820 niños muertos y 3.126 heridos. Son 820 vidas truncadas que nunca deberían haberse perdido.


En Gaza, desde octubre de 2023, las cifras oficiales indican que el ejército israelí ha matado a más de 21.000 niños y ha dejado unos 44.500 heridos hasta principios de abril de 2026. UNICEF eleva el cómputo a más de 64.000 niños muertos o heridos, incluidos unos 300 fallecidos en los 300 días posteriores al alto el fuego de octubre de 2025. Es decir, más de 25 veces el número de niños muertos en Ucrania y más de 14 veces el de heridos, en un territorio que cabe en un puñado de comarcas gallegas y en menos tiempo.


Los civiles: dos guerras, dos lógicas.


La ONU ha verificado en Ucrania al menos 16.874 civiles muertos y 51.273 heridos.


El Ministerio de Salud de Gaza cifra los muertos en 74.645 y los heridos en 175.978, según los datos más recientes, del 10 de noviembre de 2026. Mujeres y niños representan aproximadamente la mitad de las víctimas. Desde el alto el fuego de octubre de 2025 se contabilizan unos 1.600 muertos más, y siguen quedando víctimas bajo los escombros sin recuperar. Un alto el fuego en el que se sigue matando.


Quién muere en una guerra y quién muere en un exterminio.


En una guerra, la mayoría de los muertos son quienes combaten. En Ucrania, Zelenski habló en febrero de 2026 de 55.000 soldados muertos, según las cifras oficiales, mientras que el CSIS estadounidense calcula entre 125.000 y 150.000 muertos en combate hasta junio de 2026. Del lado ruso, Mediazona y la BBC han confirmado, con nombres y apellidos, unos 283.000 militares muertos, y los servicios británicos estiman la cifra en unos 500.000. Los ejércitos, quienes decidieron o acataron la guerra, ponen la inmensa mayoría de los muertos.


En Gaza, el ejército israelí reconoce 970 muertos entre soldados, reservistas y agentes de seguridad desde el 7 de octubre, 472 de ellos durante la ofensiva terrestre y 85 por fuego amigo o accidentes (el Ministerio de Defensa eleva la cifra a 1.152 con otro método de cómputo). Frente a eso, más de 74.000 palestinos muertos: unos 77 por cada militar israelí caído, según las cifras del propio ejército.


Israel afirma haber matado a más de 24.000 combatientes en Gaza. Sin embargo, una investigación de +972 Magazine y The Guardian, basada en datos de la inteligencia militar israelí, señala que, en mayo de 2025, esa misma inteligencia solo contabilizaba 8.900 combatientes de Hamás y de la Yihad Islámica como muertos o probables muertos. Israel rechaza esa interpretación. Aun así, incluso aceptando su cifra más alta, queda un número enorme de muertos que no empuñaban un fusil.


Lo que dicen los juristas.


El genocidio consiste en la comisión de determinados actos con la intención de destruir, total o parcialmente, a un grupo nacional, étnico, racial o religioso. No es una cuestión de palabras gruesas: es una categoría jurídica, y cada vez más voces con autoridad para hacerlo la aplican a Gaza.


En septiembre de 2025, la Comisión de Investigación de la ONU concluyó que Israel es responsable de genocidio en Gaza, tras constatar cuatro de los cinco actos genocidas recogidos en la Convención de 1948 y una intención de destruir a los palestinos de la Franja. Un centenar de penalistas españoles del Grupo de Estudios de Política Criminal han denunciado crímenes de guerra, de lesa humanidad y de genocidio, y reclaman a España y a la Unión Europea que se personen en los procesos penales internacionales y rompan las relaciones comerciales y diplomáticas con Israel. El caso de Sudáfrica sigue abierto ante la Corte Internacional de Justicia, y la propia Fiscalía española ha abierto una investigación.


Israel rechaza todas estas conclusiones. Que lo haga no las borra, y quienes las suscriben no son precisamente propagandistas. Quien siga poniendo en duda lo que muestran las cifras y lo que dicen los expertos será recordado por la historia como cómplice.


La diferencia no es de grado, es de naturaleza.


En una guerra, por brutal que sea, el objetivo principal no son los civiles y mucho menos los …
