author: Rizomatica
title: Machi Millaray Garrido Paillalef de territorio Lanalhue denuncia violencia racista en centro asistencial de Arauco
content:
A través de un video la Machi Millaray Garrido Paillalef denuncia trato denigrante y racista en el hospital de Arauco. Para ella y su familia este no es un hecho aislado, habiendo vivido anteriormente hechos de violencia institucional en otros centros de salud del territorio Lavkenche. La machi hace un llamado a personas y comunidades que han vivido estas situaciones a no dejarse pasar a llevar y denunciar.


Tras haber concurrido al hospital de Arauco, por una amergencia oftalmológica de su hija, derivada de Contulmo, la Machi Millaray Garrido Paillalef denunció al Dr. Cristian Castro por maltrato durante la atención.


Desde el principio de la atención ella intentó explicarle lo que le pasaba a su hija, que estaba perdiendo la visión, presentando dolor y mareos, pero el médico las ignoró durante toda la consulta, no tuvo disposición a escucharla ni a responder sus preguntas, las hizo callar en varias ocasiones y no les entregó epicrisis.


Cuando ella le solicitó al médico que pudiera derivar a su hija a neurología, él respondió de mala forma y con violencia que él no iba a dar ese tipo de horas por algo insignificante.


Al ir saliendo de la consulta, el médico en cuestión les dice:

«ustedes siempre se victimizan».


Para la machi Millaray, exite un trato racista de parte del funcionario de salud, quien actuó menospreciando su rol de machi y su tukuluwün (vestimenta tradicional) en todo momento. Y además agrega que estas situaciones son comunes para ellos, habiendo vivido violencia racista en este y otros centros de salud, durante distintas atenciones, incluso en la atención ginecológica para dar a luz a sus hijos.


“

No entiendo por qué somos maltratadas las mujeres mapuche hoy en día.


Nosotras,


a


las que nos


toca


vesti

rn

os todos los días somos las que recibimos la violencia estatal,


la violencia de la gente en las calles, que creen que somos inferiores por ser indigenas.


Ser mapuche no es algo de lo que haya que avergonzarse, es motivo de orgullo, es la dignidad misma de un pueblo que resiste manteniendo sus costumbres y tradiciones, la lengua, la salud y la educación de todo un pueblo que está vivo y presente».


Es una sumatoria de situaciones en los hospitales públicos del territorio, donde han vivido violencia y diversas situaciones de racismo institucional por su origen y por vestir su tukuluwün. Cuando no van vestidos con su vestimenta tradicional, la atención mejora un poco, comenta su familia.


«Hemos vivido diversas situaciones de racismo institucional por nuestro origen, por vestir nuestro tukuluwün, por hablar nuestra lengua. Ya es una situación inaceptable. Ser tratados como personas de segunda clase y ser tratados como terroristas solamente por vestir nuestro tukuluwün es una sumatoria de faltas de respeto que ya no son tolerables».


Según la machi, en el territorio hay muchas personas que tienen reclamos de este tipo y hace un llamado a hacer las denuncias correspondientes por todas las faltas de respeto vividas en centros de salud, de educación o de justicia. Llama a hacer las denuncias en las OIRS o donde corresponda y a no dejarse pasar a llevar como Mapuche.


“

Aquellos que hayan sido violentados en los hospitales en los colegios por su origen, por favor denuncien, existen las OIRS… En todas las comunidades es lo mismo, todos hemos vivido una mala situación en los hospitales. Existen los medios para defendernos y denunciar”.


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.

author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: Saquear y fugar: el mito del desarrollo a partir de las exportaciones
content:
Por Mariángeles Guerrero


El discurso dominante de la política económica argentina defiende la “inserción internacional” y la reprimarización de la economía. Sin embargo, un estudio reciente del

Instituto de Pensamiento y Políticas Públicas (IPyPP)

 demuestra cómo esos sectores primarios (agronegocio, minería, hidrocarburos) no solo no contribuyen al desarrollo nacional sino que, a través de las fugas de capitales, consolidan el mercado financiero global en detrimento del país donde explotan los bienes comunes. 

Molinos Agro, Minera Exar, Minas Argentinas, Pan American Energy, Tecpetrol, Pluspetrol, Vista e YPF

 son algunas de las firmas analizadas.


“La extracción de recursos naturales se articula con mecanismos de salida de divisas y una menor captación estatal de la renta generada, lo que plantea interrogantes sobre la contribución efectiva de estas actividades al desarrollo productivo nacional”, expresa el informe del IPyPP realizado por los investigadores Gustavo García Zanotti y Martín Schorr.


Que Argentina sea proveedora de materias primas (oleaginosas y cereales, minerales e hidrocarburos) y bienes derivados permitiría, según la narrativa hegemónica, aprovechar las oportunidades que ofrece la globalización y generar las divisas necesarias. Para algunas perspectivas, como la del neodesarrollismo, servirían para impulsar el desarrollo productivo. Para otras, como la del neoliberalismo, para pedalear la bicicleta de la especulación financiera. En ambos casos la base es la explotación de la naturaleza ("recursos naturales", según empresarios y funcionarios).


Pero el esquema de exportaciones “no cumple meramente una función de abastecimiento de divisas para el balance comercial, sino que funciona de manera simultánea como el principal canal de transferencia de ingresos y riqueza hacia los centros decisorios globales y las jurisdicciones de baja o nula tributación”, advierte

el estudio

.


Como resultado, indica, se configura en Argentina un extractivismo de múltiples dimensiones. No solo se extraen los recursos naturales, sino también las divisas generadas por su explotación y los ingresos fiscales que el Estado resigna mediante beneficios tributarios y regímenes promocionales (como el

Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones

, RIGI).


Foto: COFCO


Extraer y evadir


El informe explica que las grandes empresas trasladan ganancias al exterior mediante la manipulación de los precios de transferencia. Este mecanismo consiste en fijar precios para las transacciones entre empresas de un mismo grupo económico que se apartan de los que habrían acordado partes independientes en condiciones comparables. 


Por ejemplo, una filial argentina puede vender su producción a una empresa vinculada radicada en el exterior a un precio inferior al de mercado. Posteriormente, esta última puede revender la mercancía a su precio de mercado y apropiarse de la diferencia. Cuando el intermediario se encuentra radicado en una jurisdicción de baja tributación (como es el caso de Uruguay) o con escasa transparencia fiscal, esta operatoria puede facilitar el traslado de ganancias hacia el exterior y reducir la carga tributaria del grupo económico. Así disminuye la entrada de divisas al país (o, en todo caso, aumenta la salida en caso de compras o pagos de servicios).


Los sectores presentados como motores naturales del desarrollo por su capacidad para generar divisas y aprovechar las ventajas comparativas, son también espacios privilegiados para la circulación internacional del excedente. La inserción exportadora, por sí misma, no garantiza que los recursos generados permanezcan en la economía ni que se transformen en nuevas capacidades productivas.


Durante el gobierno de Javier Milei, las transferencias de ingreso hacia los sectores exportadores se intensificaron. La fuerte devaluación de fines de 2023 y la reducción de los derechos de exportación para la minería y el agronegocio favorecieron a estos sectores primario-exportadores. En 2026 se flexibilizaron las restricciones cambiarias para la remisión al exterior de utilidades generadas a partir de 2025, en un contexto en el que actividades como la petrolera y la agroindustria encabezan las remisiones de ganancias hacia el exterior.


En paralelo, el contexto internacional, signado por guerras y conflictos geopolíticos, ha reavivado las expectativas en torno a un nuevo superciclo de los precios de las materias primas, con efectos favorables sobre los ingresos y la …

author: anred
title: Quieren vender los paraísos naturales de Argentina para el turismo extranjero
content:
Parque Nacional Los Alerces (Chubut)


El gobierno de Milei se apresta a permitir la instalación de campings de lujo para ricos en áreas protegidas dentro de parques nacionales. La compañía se llama Huttopia y los proyectos corresponden a los parques nacionales Iberá (Corrientes), Iguazú (Misiones), Los Alerces (Chubut) y Los Glaciares (Santa Cruz), aunque la iniciativa puede abarcar otros lugares, con inversiones que ascienden hasta los 5 millones de euros. En el caso de Santa Cruz, el glamping (se le dice así a los campings al aire libre combinados con lujos y facilidades de hotel) quedaría ubicado en Bahía Escondida, en un sitio que fue cerrado hace más de dos décadas y prohibido por riesgo ambiental. Cerca de ahí, en la Reserva Provincial Península de Magallanes (en las inmediaciones del Perito Moreno), una empresa catarí busca establecer su complejo de 24 cabañas.

Por Nazareno Suozzi (Prensa Obrera).


Uno de los proyectos de esta empresa en Francia fue rechazado por la organización France Nature Environnement Hautes-Pyrénées, que denunció en 2022 que el estudio ambiental para el establecimiento de un camping en La Barthe-de-Neste era incompleto, con lo grave que esto era en una zona con humedales.


El objetivo del gobierno, según el ministro de Desregulación, Federico Sturzenegger, es “avanzar en un proceso de cambio para fortalecer el turismo en áreas protegidas”. Karina Milei fue quien se reunió en París con los representantes de Huttopia para delinear los detalles de la operación. De ese viaje casualmente participaron Claudio Vidal (gobernador de Santa Cruz), Ignacio Torres (Chubut) y Juan Pablo Valdés (Corrientes). Según

Tiempo

(14/11), en diciembre la empresa inaugurará un primer camping en Mar Azul (Villa Gesell, Buenos Aires).


Ya se han levantado voces en contra que no solo denuncian la entrega de los territorios para la instalación de campings de lujo, sino que advierten sobre los riesgos ambientales que acarrea una iniciativa que para llevarse adelante requiere de cierta infraestructura (suponiendo la introducción de empresas de energía, por ejemplo, en el negocio, además de otros emprendimientos comerciales) en sitios con riesgos de incendio y que fueron creados para conservar biodiversidad.


Como antecedente, en el Parque Nacional Tierra del Fuego permanecieron fondeados en Bahía Lapataia (área protegida) tres mega yates de lujo.


El gobierno prioriza los intereses sociales de un puñado de empresarios por sobre la conservación del patrimonio natural (por ejemplo, Los Alerces es reconocido por sus bosques milenarios, lagos y sus cascadas sobre el río Manso), y el turismo para ricachones mientras cada vez más trabajadores deben privarse de vacacionar en algún lugar debido al deterioro sostenido de los salarios.


La iniciativa es una expresión a escala más pequeña de lo que quiso hacer con el por ahora frustrado proyecto de modificación de la ley de tierras. Ya hay una cantidad considerable de

empresarios cataríes y franceses

 que poseen hectáreas en Argentina.


Motosierra


El gobierno avanza por este camino mientras desguaza la Administración de Parques Nacionales y ataca a sus trabajadores, que denuncian que “hay despidos inducidos” por el congelamiento salarial imperante. En mayo, el gobierno recortó 2.577 millones de pesos del presupuesto de la APN. El Parque Nacional Nahuel Huapí tuvo un recorte de 191 millones y Los Alerces (que sufrió incendios forestales) uno de 70 millones. El ajuste afecta fundamentalmente gastos operativos como el mantenimiento de vehículos, servicios técnicos y suministros básicos (

Fundación Terram

).


Por otro lado, está ajustando los fondos destinados a emergencias e incendios. El Presupuesto 2027 estipula, para la Subsecretaría de Ambiente, fondos que están casi un 85% por debajo de los niveles de 2023. Al Fondo Nacional para el Enriquecimiento y la Conservación de los Bosques Nativos, por su parte, le asignan recursos «25 veces menores a los establecidos por ley» (

Tiempo

, ídem). Desde el Parque Nacional Calilegua denunciaron que los tijeretazos presupuestarios supusieron la reducción de guardaparques, brigadistas, vehículos y equipamiento; el parque cuenta con menos de 30 trabajadores para proteger 76.000 hectáreas de tierra (

Somos Jujuy

, 15/5).


Quien promueve toda esta política de la mano de Milei es Sergio Martín Álvarez, presidente de la APN. Reemplazó a Cristian Larden, bajo cuya gestión tuvieron lugar los mayores incendios en la Patagonia …

title: Prisoner Newroz Bozkurt brought to hospital
content:
Newroz Bozkurt, who suffers from Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL), was transferred to Etlik City Hospital on Saturday, 14 November, after becoming unwell.


Newroz Bozkurt has been in detention since January 1999 and was diagnosed with leukaemia in June.


It was reported that Newroz Bozkurt had previously been taken to Etlik City Hospital in December 2025. Despite medical examinations revealing that her blood levels were low, no medical intervention was carried out. It was subsequently reported that her lawyers filed a criminal complaint against the doctor concerned.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Int’l groups show solidarity to Filipinos vs Pax Silica
content:
International progressive groups have launched their own protest actions, standing in solidarity with Filipinos as they campaign against the United States (US)-led Pax Silica initiative.


These mobilizations, led by the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS), the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines (ICHRP), Migrante International, and BAYAN International, to name a few, were held in 23 cities across 14 countries, as the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit kicked off in Metro Manila on November 15.


Street demonstrations were launched by Philippine progressive groups due to the expected visit of US President Donald Trump, which resulted in the

violent dispersal and arrest

 of more than 300 people, including journalists and campus journalists.


Read:

Int’l groups condemn police brutality


“This is the real face of Marcos Jr.’s rule: fascism, subservience, and a sellout to imperialist dictates,” Azra Sayeed, ILPS secretary-general, said in a statement sent to the media.


Progressive groups stage an anti-Pax Silica protests in New Zealand (left) and Hong Kong (right). Contributed photos


The proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park (CAMP), a 1,600-hectare industrial hub, is planned to be constructed in New Clark City, Tarlac, under the Pax Silica initiative, designating the facility as an economic security zone (ESZ) that would strengthen shared supply chains in semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies.


Indigenous peoples and peasant communities in the area would be affected if the plan pushes through.


Sharanya Nayak of Indigenous Peoples’ Land Life and Knowledge Collective (IPLLK), a grassroots advocacy network in India, echoed the assertions that the Pax Silica initiative would only bring environmental destruction. “The reality is that extraction of these minerals is at the cost of indigenous peoples’ lands and identities.”


India became a Pax Silica signatory after it signed the declaration with the US on February 20, nearly two months before the Philippines’ participation on April 16. 


There are 25 Pax Silica declaration signatories, according to the official website of the US government, while Taiwan was listed as a non-signatory participant. 


Progressive groups stage an anti-Pax Silica protest in Türkiye. Contributed photo


Before the ASEAN Summit, the signing of the initiative’s framework had been targeted during Trump’s expected visit. But it has been confirmed that there was no signing during the summit, with the state-run Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) saying that negotiations with the US are still ongoing.


Read:


‘Make Pax Silica deal public’


“The Marcos regime is no doubt enraged that the people will resist and stand up and fight against the continued colonization of their country,” Sayeed said.

(DAA)

author: Kodao Productions
title: Revolutionary groups urge Filipinos to hold Trump accountable over war crimes
content:
The National Democratic Front of the Philippines (NDFP) said US President Donald Trump’s visit to the Philippines would deepen US involvement in the country and serve the foreign country’s interests in Philippine land, resources and labor.


NDFP secretary general Elias Dipasupil in a statement also described the US-led Pax Silica initiative as an escalation in US intervention and oppression in the Philippines.


“Trump, a certified warmonger, is an enemy of peace in the Philippines,” Dipasupil said, adding that the US only seeks to draw the country into conflict with China through increased US military aid and joint US-PH military activities that are also used to suppress the revolutionary movement in the


NDFP allied organizations — Compatriots, an organization of overseas Filipinos; KAGUMA, Alliance of Patriotic Teachers; and Christians for National Liberation (CNL) – said Ferdinand Marcos Jr. government’s subservience to US dictates would only result in economic hardship, resource plunder and violations to Philippine sovereignty.


Compatriots said US domination in the Philippines only worsened economic pressures that lead many Filipinos to seek work abroad. It cited “landlessness, lack of job opportunities, livelihood, low wages and high costs of living.”


KAGUMA criticized projects promoted as sources of jobs, renewable energy and participation in the global artificial-intelligence supply chain which, it said only serve the economic and military interests of the US. It warned that resource extraction could damage the environment, displace Indigenous communities, and intensify landgrabbing.


The group also urged educators to build and promote critical awareness. “Education is a key platform for fostering patriotic awareness,” the underground organization said.


CNL chairperson Renmin Malaya described Trump’s politics as marked by “chaos, militarism, imperial aggression” and called for an independent economy.


He said the Philippines should “develop its own productive capabilities, protect its patrimony, and firmly uphold its sovereignty.” Malaya said that liberation requires militant struggle and cited the international-law concept of

jus ad bellum

 (just war), “to end oppression and exploitation.”


CPP condemns mass arrests of anti-Trump patriots


The Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP), meanwhile, said it stands with Filipinos in absolute condemnation of the widespread mass arrests carried out by the Philippine National Police since Sunday that targeted workers, students, peasants, Indigenous peoples and other sectors who defy Trump and Pax Silica.


The CPP also condemned the arrest of scores of journalists covering the protest actions, as well as paralegals providing assistance.


“The mass arrests, purportedly carried out with so-called maximum tolerance, exposes the Marcos regime’s gross intolerance to protest actions that oppose his subservience to his American masters,” CPP chief information officer Marco Valbuena said.


“Police actions have been coordinated with US Secret Service agents who are in the country ahead of Trump. Marcosian political repression, along with artificial white walls erected to hide impoverished communities, are reminiscent of his father’s old dystopian dictatorship,” Valbuena added.


By ordering the police to forcibly clamp down on all protests, Marcos clearly aims to please his imperialist master Trump that may be a prelude to even more brutal acts of suppression that will drive away communities to pave the way for imperialist plunder of the country’s patrimony, CPP said.


“Contrary to Marcos’ aims, however, intensified fascist repression is certain to succeed only in fueling greater resistance of the Filipino people to US imperialism’s Pax Silica with its aims of expanding its economic and geopolitical interests in the Philippines,” Valbuena warned. #

(B. Libres and Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Brian Hioe
title: Ahead of Elections, KMT Elders Outline Ten-Year Plan on Unification at Sun Yat-Sen Commemoration
content:
AT AN EVENT in Taipei on November 12th, organized by a number of senior KMT officials to commemorate the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen, a ten-year plan for the political unification of Taiwan and China was set out. Over 250 individuals were in attendance at the event.

Given that the media cycle in Taiwan is focused on the upcoming local elections, there was relatively little attention to this news item. Nevertheless, among those in attendance at the event were former KMT Taipei mayoral candidate Ting Shou-chung, former KMT majority speaker Wang Jinpyng, and Su Chi, who is considered the architect of the 1992 Consensus. As such, a former premier, former Legislative Yuan head, former Examination Yuan head, and former legislators were among those in attendance.

The ten-year plan for the political unification of Taiwan and China was phrased as part of a “Cross-Strait Peace Initiative” with specific benchmarks. In 2027, a referendum to grant the government the power to conduct negotiations with China would be initiated by a KMT-controlled Legislative Yuan. In 2028, the KMT would return to power by winning the presidency. In 2030, market integration between Taiwan and China will occur. In 2032, a unified currency would be adopted between Taiwan and China. In 2036, discussions would be held on unification, which would include possibly adopting “One Country, Two Systems”. “One Country, Two Systems” would be considered one of a number of possible proposals that would be adopted. Five working groups were set up at the event to facilitate unification, on cross-strait security, economic development, cultural and youth exchanges, governance, and peaceful unification and development.

As KMT Taipei mayoral candidate Chiang Wan-an and outgoing Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen sent flowers to the event, it has been questioned whether they meant to tacitly endorse the proceedings. At the event, comments included the view that Taiwanese are Chinese, as well as that the Republic of China is China.

Likewise, it has been noted by observers that, on the same day in Beijing, Chinese President Xi Jinping also held activities to commemorate the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen. In speeches, Xi stated that “the complete unification of the motherland must and will be achieved.” Xi also stated that “One Country, Two Systems” was still the framework for unification.

It proves somewhat of a mystery as to why Ting, Wang, Su, and other KMT heavyweights who participated in the event felt the need to hold such an event. It is generally thought that KMT chair Cheng Li-wun has alienated the public through expressing pro-unification views on many occasions, such that many KMT candidates are reluctant to make public appearances with her for fear that this will impact their electoral chances.

Likewise, local elections are fundamentally about local issues, and not cross-strait issues, which is part of why the KMT does better in local elections than national elections. It is not tactically advisable for the KMT to create opportunities for a cross-strait frame to intrude in local elections.

But absences from the event are notable, precisely in that hardline pro-unification figures such as Cheng Li-wun and current KMT legislative caucus leader Fu Kun-chi were not present. Figures such as Ting and Su have mostly been out of the limelight in past years, as party elders who are not active political candidates. It is possible that the move is aimed at cementing a historical legacy, as elders who helped facilitate unification, or occurs because such elders are seeking to have some influence over the current course of the party–or that such elders are angling for Beijing’s support in order to return to active political life by routing around Cheng, Fu, and other figures who are active participants in today’s electoral politics.

In this sense, it is unclear whether the event reflects the views of the KMT writ large–and certainly, it proves electorally inadvisable for the KMT to remind the public of cross-strait concerns shortly before local elections. Ting, Wang, and Su have, in fact, simply given the DPP political ammunition in the local elections with their actions. Nevertheless, their actions still prove concerning, especially if they are angling for Chinese support as part of efforts to realize some ten-year plan at the end of which would see the erosion of democratic governance in Taiwan.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Overcoming police brutality, protests continue vs. Trump, Pax Silica
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates held an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

“Even if we see police harassment, it does not deter us. We will persevere and fight back.”

No amount of police brutality could hold back the progressive groups from continuing their protest today, November 16. They gathered at the Liwasang Bonifacio and strongly condemned the Marcos Jr. administration for its subservience to foreign interests.

“We feel more courage now that there are many people who chose to stand alongside our fight for our ancestral lands,” Ayta elder Nelson De Guzman told Bulatlat in Filipino. “Even if we see police harassment, it does not deter us. We will persevere and fight back.”

De Guzman is among the delegation of the Ayta-Hungey community from Capas, Tarlac who went to Manila to join the series of protests against the arrival of U.S. President Donald Trump and the reported signing of the Pax Silica framework agreement.

He said, “They are lying when they said that indigenous peoples will not be affected [by Pax Silica]. We are here to prove them wrong and stand for what is right.”

The first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit on November 15 began with a series of arbitrary mass arrests of close to 300 activists, students, journalists, and community leaders.

Hundreds of the arrested individuals were part of the Lakbayan Southern Tagalog who were supposed to hold a campout in Liwasang Bonifacio to attend the series of protests in Manila.

They have been detained for more than 24 hours at Camp Bagong Diwa in Bicutan.

Read: Police violently disperse, arrest hundreds in Muntinlupa protest

Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code limits detention without charges to 12 [light penalties], 18,[correctional penalties] or 36 hours [capital penalties]. It also guarantees the accused’s right to legal counsel at any time.

Lawyers, paralegals, and human rights investigators were only allowed entry to Camp Bagong Diwa after six hours of negotiation with the police.

“From the first day since we started our lakbayan (collective march), the repression never stopped. They tried to sabotage our program, the wheels of our vehicles, up to the massive deployment of police officers within our camp-out area,” human rights defender Paul Tagle, who is part of the Southern Tagalog delegation, said in Filipino in a press conference.

He said that detained individuals are being threatened with charges under the Public Assembly Act (Batas Pambansa Blg. 880), a remnant of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.’s dictatorship, which he described as a complete “madness” since it is the police who exercised violent intervention.

Read: Bayan hits ‘Marcosian’ tactics against protesters

At least 500 policemen are reportedly stationed in the entry and exit points in University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City, where some 200 Ayta and their supporters held a campout.

Cristina Palabay, secretary general of human rights group Karapatan, demanded accountability from police officers and commanders who ordered the violent interference. She emphasized that the denial coming from state security forces, particularly the National Police Commission (Napolcom), rings hollow as the police brutality was properly documented by the journalists and activists, publicized in the social media.

“The fact is,” said Palabay, “the PNP has long been besmirching the uniform. Yesterday’s incidents of police brutality have not been the first, nor will they be the last, given the vociferous statements issued by the PNP’s talking heads, and their consistent denials of the truth.”

Moreover, the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) said that neither the ASEAN Summit nor Trump’s visit guarantees the suspension of peoples’ right to protest and peaceful assembly.

“The Constitution guarantees the people’s right to protest. Peaceful assembly is no crime, while the law requires maximum tolerance and protects participants in otherwise peaceful assemblies from criminal liability,” the NUPL said in a statement.

The group also demanded release of the detained individuals, the police to pull back from UP’s gates to allow the protest delegation to reach the assembly sites unharmed, and the accountability of state security personnel responsible for unlawful arrests and assaults.

author: rti_admin
title: Building Safe Spaces: Women’s Safety Must Mean More Than Protection
content:
A safe workplace is not defined only by the absence of harassment. It is also a place where women can speak, disagree, seek support, and participate in decisions without fear.

We often assume that organizations are safe places because they have rules, policies, and systems in place. But is that enough? A workplace may have a policy against sexual harassment and a committee to receive complaints, yet a woman may still hesitate to speak because she fears being judged, ignored, or facing consequences. This makes me ask a simple question: what does it really mean for a woman to feel safe at work?

Safety is usually understood as protection from harm, injury, or danger. In a workplace, that includes physical safety and freedom from sexual harassment. But it also includes something less visible: the freedom to express an opinion, raise concern, disagree with a colleague, or ask for help without fear of humiliation or retaliation. A woman may be physically safe in an office and still feel unsafe if she cannot speak openly. For me, women’s safety is connected to dignity. It is about being able to work without fear, but also about being treated as a human being whose experiences, feelings, and responsibilities matter.

Physical safety means being protected from violence, injury, threats and other forms of bodily harm. It also includes a safe working environment, appropriate security arrangements, transport where required and access to help in an emergency. Sexual safety means being free from unwanted sexual comments, gestures, messages, touching, harassment and violence. Everyone should be able to decide what happens to their body and should not have to tolerate unwanted behaviour as part of working life. Economic safety includes fair wages, equal opportunities and the ability to earn a livelihood without exploitation or threats. Social and organizational safety means being treated fairly and respectfully, without discrimination, bullying or harassment based on gender, caste, colour or social background.

Psychological safety is equally important. It means being able to express thoughts, ask questions, raise concerns, share ideas and admit mistakes without fear of humiliation or punishment. Amy Edmondson has described it as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Earlier work by Edgar Schein and Warren Bennis in 1965 also discussed psychological safety in relation to organisational learning and change. The central idea is straightforward: people should be able to speak honestly, ask for help and participate without worrying that they will be mocked, ignored or penalised. Psychological safety does not mean avoiding disagreement or accountability. It means that people can engage in difficult conversations without being degraded or threatened.

Safety should be a basic right, not a privilege available only in certain places or under certain conditions. Article 21 of the Constitution of India protects the right to life and personal liberty, and the right to live with dignity has been recognised as part of this constitutional protection. Yet many women continue to experience harassment, discrimination and fear in daily life. When women do not feel safe, the effects go beyond the immediate risk of harm. They may limit their movements, avoid certain jobs, turn down opportunities involving travel or give up professional goals. Insecurity can affect confidence, mental well-being, economic independence and participation in society. It becomes a barrier to equality and empowerment.

For many women, fear begins long before they reach the office. Roads, bus stops, railway stations, public transport, markets and the route home are all part of the working day. Some think twice before travelling alone, returning late or visiting an unfamiliar place. Some ask a father, brother, male relative or friend to accompany them because they believe another person’s presence may protect them from unwanted attention. Instead of feeling free to move independently, they make arrangements simply to feel secure.

A baseline household survey conducted in Delhi in October and November 2012 offers a stark illustration of this fear. The study, carried out by the International Center for Research on Women (ICRW) as part of the Safe Cities programme with UN Women and local partners, found that only 5% of women and girls surveyed ranked public spaces in Delhi as safe from sexual violence. This is sometimes summarized as 95% feeling …

author: Agatha Hazel Rabino
title: Press freedom advocates condemn police brutality as 20 media workers nabbed while covering ASEAN protests
content:
At least 20 media workers from various campus publications and community media outfits were arrested while on coverage on Sunday, November 15, at Sucat People’s Park Muntinlupa.

The journalists were covering the Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan which was originally set to continue towards the Kampuhan in Liwasang Bonifacio today. Mass arrests have followed while the organizers of the group were still in the middle of negotiating with the police to let them continue their protest.

As of press time, publication members from the UPLB Perspective, The Staple, Philippine Collegian, CCC The Sentinel were confirmed to be among those arrested. Meanwhile, 3 journalists from Southern Tagalog Exposure (STex), 3 coordinators from College Editors Guild of the Philippines ST and journalists from Parañaque and UP Baguio were also apprehended.

Alternative media alliance Altermidya Network condemned the police violence against the protesters and journalists.

“These incidents raise serious concerns about the safety of journalists covering public demonstrations and the conduct of police operations during the ASEAN Summit,” the network said in a statement.

Altermidya also added that several cases of harassment and manhandling of journalists were also documented during the morning protest at Liwasang Bonifacio.

“The government cannot claim to uphold democratic freedoms before the international community while police forces suppress public demonstrations and interfere with journalists documenting events on the ground. Security preparations for an international gathering do not suspend constitutional rights. Freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, and press freedom must be respected, including when citizens express opposition to government policies and international agreements,” it furthered.

Meanwhile, the College Editors Guild of the Philippines (CEGP) also condemned the police operations against protesters and members of the campus press.

“The Guild vehemently condemns the mass arrests carried out by state forces, as these constitute clear violations of press freedom and attempts to suppress coverage of Lakbayan and Kampuhan, where people from different sectors are expressing their rejection of Pax Silica and Trump’s visit.

These mass arrests, acts of hamletting, intimidation harassment and attempted arrests for over 24 hours are deliberate crackdowns on freedom of expression. Not only are those who participate in the protests being targeted, but publications that highlight the grassroot struggle of those who are affected by Pax Silica. This stems from Marcos’ overkill order of police deployment to silence peaceful dissent,” CEGP said.

Following the arrests, press freedom advocates called for the immediate and unconditional release of journalists and protesters nabbed during the police operations.

“We demand that the Philippine National Police disclose the whereabouts and legal status of all those arrested, guarantee their safety, and ensure their immediate access to legal counsel. We also demand an independent investigation into the arrests, the harassment and manhandling of media workers, the attempted arrests of campus journalists, and other reported acts of police violence against journalists and protesters. Police personnel found responsible for unlawful actions must be held accountable,” it said.

It also called for the support of fellow media organizations, campus publications, press freedom advocates, and other human rights group to stand with their detained and harassed colleagues and to defend the people’s right to know.

author: Nick Everett
title: Remembering the Santa Cruz massacre
content:
Thirty-five years ago, Indonesian elite Kopassus troops opened fire on a peaceful procession in Dili, the capital of then Indonesian-occupied East Timor (today known as Timor Leste), killing hundreds. The Indonesian generals responsible have never faced justice, protected by the Western governments who armed them and abetted their crimes. 

The procession, on the morning of 12 November 1991, followed a memorial mass at Motael Church for Sebastião Gomes Rangel, a young Timorese man killed by Indonesian security forces two weeks earlier. As the procession of 3,000 mourners made its way to Santa Cruz cemetery, pro-independence banners and flags were unfurled. Minutes after the crowd arrived at the cemetery, troops opened fire without warning.

Shooting continued as people tried to scale the cemetery’s high walls. Some were shot in the back while running away. Others while seeking shelter behind tombstones or in the cemetery’s chapel. More were stabbed and shot as they lay on the ground in pools of blood. According to survivor testimonies, dozens more were executed or disappeared after being taken to the Wira Husada Military Hospital. 

At least 271 East Timorese were killed that day, and an equal number disappeared, believed dead, according to the East Timor Action Network.

Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans was quick to defend Indonesia’s military, which had invaded East Timor in December 1975 and maintained a brutal occupation of the former Portuguese colony. A month after the massacre, Evans

told

 parliament that while the incident was “‘deplorable”, it “was not ... a calculated or deliberate act of the [Indonesian] government as such”. Rather, it was “the product of aberrant behaviour by a subgroup within the country”. 

Two years earlier, Evans had joined his Indonesian counterpart, Ali Alatas, to toast the signing of the Timor Gap Treaty in a plane above the Timor Sea. With a glass of champagne in his hand, Evans declared: “This is a uniquely historical moment that is truly, uniquely historical”.

The treaty, several years in the making, carved up the rich oil and gas resources beneath the Timor Sea and opened the way for their exploitation by Australian resource companies. 

The Santa Cruz massacre was not unique. Many had preceded it, including the Kraras massacres, in the southern municipality of Viqueque in 1983. Prabowo Subianto, a rising star in the army and the son-in-law of Indonesian dictator, General Suharto, commanded the Kopassus special forces unit responsible. 

The Kraras massacres have been

compared

 with the US army’s massacre of Vietnamese civilians in the village of Mai Lai in 1968. Much like the strategy pursued by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon, such attacks sought to isolate combatants via major military operations that killed and displaced large numbers of civilians.

In 2005, East Timor’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (CAVR)

concluded

 that Indonesia’s 24-year-long occupation resulted in between 102,800 and 183,000 conflict-related deaths, alongside widespread systematic torture, unlawful killings, enforced disappearances, forced displacement, and sexual violence. Many human rights organisations, including

Genocide Watch

, argue that Indonesia committed a genocide in East Timor.

What made the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre different from those that preceded it was that it was caught on

film

. When British cameraman Max Stahl’s footage was subsequently broadcast, it shone a light on Indonesia’s crimes and revived a global solidarity movement.

In Australia in the 1990s, socialists led a campaign group called Action in Solidarity with Indonesia and East Timor (ASIET), which coordinated demonstrations in conjunction with other East Timor solidarity groups across the country to commemorate the Santa Cruz massacre on 12 November each year.

We argued that the overthrow of Indonesia’s military dictatorship would open the road to Timorese independence, and that we therefore needed to support not only the resistance to the occupation, but also the growing student and worker movements in Indonesia that were calling for an end to Suharto’s military rule. We demanded that our own government break military ties with Indonesia.

Military and diplomatic ties between the two countries were extensive and growing, and by 1996 included a military pact. At the time, Australia was training Kopassus forces at the Kokoda Barracks on the Gold Coast. The Keating government also shamefully (and …

author: Kerry Smith
title: NSW Education minister urged to reinstate pro-Palestine NSW teacher John Morris
content:
The NSW Department of Education is penalising teachers for showing solidarity with Palestine and taking a stand against genocide.

John Morris, a teacher of more than 30 years, was suspended without pay, after News Corp’s Daily Telegraph ran a smear campaign on Morris’ support for the right of Palestinian to resist genocide.

The Daily Telegraph notified the NSW Department of Education about Morris’ posts on X, on September 18 and the Department of Education suspended him the following day.

“This is a witch hunt and trail by media,” said Teachers and School Staff for Palestine. Morris is a long-standing member of the NSW Teachers Federation and life member and former president and secretary of the Canterbury-Bankstown Teachers Association.

The department is investigating Morris’ posts.

The Daily Telegraph is falsely accused Morris of being a supporter of a “terrorist organisation”, Hamas. One of the “offensive” posts quoted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who said the following in 2019: “Anyone who wants to thwart the establishment of a Palestinian state has to support bolstering Hamas and transferring money to Hamas … This is part of our strategy — to isolate the Palestinians in Gaza from the Palestinians in the West Bank.”

The political atmosphere enabling this witch-hunt has been created by the NSW Labor government. Premier Chris Minns has indicated his support for banning pro-Palestinian slogans “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free”, and “Globalise the intifada”.

NSW Labor has also introduced draconian anti-protest laws, to try and stop people from expressing their support for Palestinians’ right to self-determination.

The United Nations General Assembly in 1990 endorsed the right for national liberation movements to employ “all available means, including armed struggle” to resist colonial domination, in Resolution 45/130.

Other teachers, including Wasim Al-Haj, has been forced out of a school for wearing a keffiyeh. He is suing the Department of Education for racial discrimination. Other teachers have been warned not to wear Palestinian cultural items.

However, the department was forced to publicly apologise to a student of Palestinian dissent after he was banned from attending his formal wearing a keffiyeh.

The Teachers and School Staff for Palestine is organising an action at the Industrial Relations Commission, at 10 Smith Street, Parramatta, on November 30 at 10am calling for Morris to be reinstated.

The group is also demanding that the Department of Education end its discrimination against teachers supporting Palestinian human rights.

author: @ndy
title: The struggle is real with Jillian Segal.
content:
See also : Jillian Segal and husband funding far-right group “Advance”, Anthony Klan, The Klaxon, July 12, 2025.

Jillian Segal — the South African–born Australian lawyer, business executive, and Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism — recently dropped another Report, ASECA Priorities. According to the Special Envoy, a newly-hatched “modern progressive antisemitism” … is taking “the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes”.

My first reaction on reading this passage was to recall the unforgettable 2014 framing by the Australian Defence League of the alleged “evil anarcho-pinko-anarchist-islamic cabal of dirt”; the wicked coalition then allegedly intent on turning Penrith into a no-go zone for patriots.

In any case, inre the Report, Jeffrey Loewenstein doesn’t hold back in It’s time to sack Jillian Segal (Deepcut News, November 2, 2026), the Jewish Council of Australia (October 30, 2026) has slammed it, and Jeff Sparrow has characterised it, not unfairly, as a Trumpian plan to curtail free speech (Crikey, November 2, 2026). The Report is also subject to critical scrutiny by Robert Manne, who examines it in On the Rise of Antisemitism in Australia (November 8, 2026), along with the thoughts of Lord Andrew Roberts and Sir Simon Schama on the subject of ‘antisemitism’. Manne concludes that:

Schama believes he can help combat the rise of antisemitism in the Diaspora by defending the indefensible, the war crimes of the IDF under Benjamin Netanyahu. I believe a more likely remedy would be for leading Diaspora thinkers, like Schama, and influential publishers, like Morry Schwartz, and the leaders in Australia of the principal Israel and Jewish lobbies, like Jillian Segal, to speak the truth about what, under Netanyahu and the two Kahanist-fascist members of his Government, Israel has become, and the moral revolution that has to happen in Israel if Jews in the Diaspora are to be spared from the dreadful rise of antisemitism that is spreading around the Western world.

FWIW, for over 20 years I’ve been attempting, inter alia, to monitor and document organised, public expressions of antisemitism and other racisms in Australia — the better to disrupt it. I’m also an anarchist, and one of many people to hold the view that the Israeli state has engaged in a genocidal assault upon Palestine in the three years since October 7 (the latest chapter in a much longer history of deadly state violence). On that basis, I assume that Segal et. al. would categorise myself as an exponent of ‘far-left antisemitism’, the meaning of which is elaborated upon in this passage:

Far-left antisemitism or issue-motivated antisemitism

Far-left ideology and associated activism feature a worldview that casts the world in terms of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed’. Within this binary framework, Israel is portrayed as a colonial project that is inherently racist and Jews who support Israel’s existence are portrayed as representatives of ‘whiteness’ (regardless of their ethnicity), privilege (regardless of their means), imperialism (notwithstanding the absence of an empire), greedy capitalism and the projection of Western power.

This framing allows longstanding antisemitic motifs to be repackaged in the academic language of anti-racism, decolonisation, human rights, social justice and intersectionality, often in service of a traditional Marxist revolutionary agenda.

When a cause is believed – with ideological fervour – to be absolutely just, its ends can come to justify any means and its adherents can feel free to vilify, harass and seek to destroy those who associate with what is framed as evil.

Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes – apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc. – has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.

In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest.

The strange – but …

author: Bizzi Lavelle
title: Young Women, Pain, Mobility Aids
content:
Stories Contributors Pitch an Idea

To be sick, or have a health condition of any kind is not a moral failing. I know this and I hope that you do too. However, every time I find myself staying in or leaving something early because I’m in pain or I’m fatigued, I can’t help but feel the people around me are disappointed.

People wish they had a friend who could come to their fortnightly event like they said they would. They wish they could book a performer to MC an event without them withdrawing due to spending that week pain ridden in bed. They wish the friend they extended a birthday party invite made it instead of sending through an apologetic message. They wish their friend would be in the room cheering them on at their weekly drag comp or production show.

A common online talking point echoes in my head as I send my latest “I’m sorry” message; you have to inconvenience yourself a little for the sake of your community. You have to be someone’s villager if you want to have a village.

With the weeks or days I spend hidden away, inside, barely leaving the house I often ask myself, do I deserve to be in anyone’s village? Do I deserve my own villagers?

The words to Rina Sawayama’s ‘Bad Friend’ circle my mind as I spend another Saturday night in my pajamas, watching anime in bed: “So don’t ask me where I’ve been, been avoiding everything.”

As I’m lamenting my woes to my notes app and the friends who get it, an article from The Times UK comes across my feed. “Why are young women using walking sticks?” by Katherine Stock. And then another, this time from The Telegraph, “How having a disability became cool” by Poppy Coburn.

The themes of these pieces are misogyny and ableism, with sprinkles of transphobia and ageism.

In both of these pieces, the authors seem to believe that young women in increasing numbers are faking to be disabled for social clout. In the first piece, Stock declares young women using mobility aids and posting about being ill are victims of “social contagion” deems the pain they’re in as “unclear” and therefore “unclear” if these women “really have” disabilities.

It’s wild to me, that in 2026, anyone would partake in such ableist vitriol. Despite what both authors think, there are a wide range of ways to be disabled. Disability and chronic illness don’t always look like a wheelchair user. Sometimes disabilities and chronic illnesses are invisible. Sometimes they’re dynamic. The only criteria to being disabled is having a condition, injury or alike that impedes you and your ability to do day to day tasks.

Disability is the only minority group a person can become part of at a moment’s notice, and is the only minority group we will all be part of at some point in our lives. As my friend, Protect our NDIS rally organiser and activist Oriela says “You will become disabled. That’s a promise not just a threat”.

That one influencer you follow could one day be surfing and the next using a wheelchair or cane. You aren’t able to discern how much pain someone is in by simply looking at them. If that were the case, women wouldn’t be waiting years for their pain to be believed and diagnosed.

For Aboriginal women, seeking medical care has an extra layer of stress. Racial bias in medicine historically saw beliefs that bla(c)k people, particularly women, have a higher pain tolerance than their white counterparts. This, along with classic medical misogyny has led to Aboriginal women being mistreated, ignored or treated as though they’re only ‘drug seeking’.

In Allanah Hunt’s 2024 piece ‘The Good Patient’, she details her experiences of medical racism as she navigates dealing with endometriosis. Despite Allanah’s attempts to present to hospitals as the best and most polite patient, her pain was still disbelieved and she was still treated as a drug seeker. “Because the truth is, no matter how much I’m ‘the good patient’, I will never escape the racial judgement from healthcare providers” Allanah writes.

Similarly, Colleen Lavelle (my mother) discusses her experience of medical racism in her 2017 piece. “Death by racism: bigotry in the health system is harming Indigenous patients’”.

She notes from her own experiences and other First Nations people whose medical experiences she’s listened to that a common thread is wondering if you’ve been overly sensitive.

One memory I have from my teens is when I was at the shops with my mum and younger sister. I went out to the car to put some bags in the car and a man …

author: Editors
title: Historic Victorian election an opportunity to rebuild socialist organisation
content:
The Victorian election will be a significant moment in Australian politics. 

The ALP, which has ruled the state for most of the last three decades, looks set to take a significant hit to its primary vote. A DemosAU poll has Labor’s primary vote at 18 percent, just one point ahead of the Greens. Resolve’s reporting had them at 22 percent, which is nevertheless a record low and well down on the 37 percent primary vote they received in the 2022 state election.

Meanwhile, far-right One Nation has entered the political field as a serious challenger to the major parties, if polling is accurate. The once-pariah party is now firmly part of the mainstream, as are its fascist-adjacent politics. And the Liberals, who last election were declared too “weak and divided” and facing too serious an “identity crisis” to govern by the

Age

, now enjoy the backing of almost all the corporate media. 

The much more dispersed nature of the vote makes the outcome difficult to predict. 

Labor’s leaders have essentially given up on winning; every MP is now in a desperate fight to save their own seat and career. The union movement has largely abandoned the field, with a number belatedly refusing to campaign for Labor.

Even the premier is looking likely to lose his seat. Good riddance.

Carroll’s strategy of shifting the party hard to the right by attacking the CFMEU and boosting the spectre of youth crime is backfiring, alienating what little support the ALP had left. His short time in office will be quickly forgotten, but his legacy—of demoralising working-class Labor voters and legitimising the various attacks the incoming Liberal government has planned—will remain. 

In his place will step Jess Wilson as the head of a resurgent Liberal Party. Her plan is there for all to see. Savage cuts to the public service. A ban on protests without police permission. Censorship of the pro-Palestine movement. Ripping up the Treaty.

Wilson has promised to recall parliament before Christmas, not to address housing affordability or the crisis in our hospitals, but to introduce harsher bail laws and put more kids in jail. All of this she’s hoping to do in a Trump-style 100-day blitz, during which she will serve as both premier and treasurer.

Wilson has been sold to the public as a moderate, a relatable millennial and a fresh face. The capitalist press, including the

 Age

and the

Guardian

,


have done their bit to popularise this image.

Her history suggests something quite different. She has been a Liberal apparatchik since her university days at Monash, after which she worked at disgraced consultancy firm KPMG, before jumping ship to be a policy executive at the Business Council of Australia.

Her Institute of Public Affairs-aligned husband stood down as a Liberal candidate in 2014 after it was revealed he referred to gay men as “faggots”. They remain happily married.

The truth is that Wilson is a trained class warrior for the billionaires and the bosses. Aside from the culture wars and the

UFC fight nights

, the key goal of her campaign is to balance the state’s budget and cut taxes on the corporate elite.

The blatant contradiction between these two goals can only be resolved through swingeing cuts to health care, education and other vital public services, mass sackings and the privatisation of state assets. She has already flagged her desire to do both, though the financial press are demanding that she cut much harder and deeper.

In addition to the prospect of a slash-and-burn, Kennett-style Liberal government, workers will face a One Nation party that is set to win an unprecedented vote. These far-right nutters will exercise a constant rightward pressure on the Liberals, particularly when the latter seek to pass legislation through the upper house, where One Nation may well hold the balance of power. They will also use their platform to attack the rights of workers and women while demonising migrants and other oppressed groups.

But while official politics is shifting sharply to the right, there are plenty of people looking for an alternative. Despite the tidal wave of establishment hostility directed at the Greens because of the party’s strong stance on Gaza, they look set for a meaningful increase in their primary vote.

More importantly for the radical left, the Victorian Socialists campaign has been easily the biggest yet. More than 2,000 people have participated in public meetings, door knocks, phone banks and rallies across the …

author: Yasmine Johnson
title: Jillian Segal’s war on the left
content:
Antisemitism Special Envoy Jillian Segal’s “Plan to combat antisemitism” is nothing of the sort. Her latest report, published 30 October, is a stunning piece of Trumpist propaganda. It is riddled with conspiracy theories about malign radical-left and Islamist influence in Australian institutions. It calls for sweeping crackdowns on free speech, political activism and migration, all in the name of protecting Israel’s reputation. It is an indictment of the Labor government that commissioned it.

Labor named Segal “special envoy to combat antisemitism” knowing her record as a right-wing warrior and campaigner for Israel’s murderous wars. Her appointment was part of a multi-faceted offensive against the Palestine solidarity movement. She has consistently used this platform to shield the Israeli government from criticism and attack opponents of the war.

Segal’s new report pays little attention to the growing antisemitic far right. Since her appointment, Nazis have addressed thousands at anti-migrant marches. One Nation, a party

riddled with Hitler fanatics

, has shot up in the polls. But far-right antisemitism is minimised because it isn’t the “primary source of concern or anxiety to members of the Jewish community”.

The real danger is “modern, progressive antisemitism”, which Segal labels “the most pervasive manifestation of antisemitism facing Australia”. 

Segal claims that anti-Israel progressives have simply repackaged an age-old hatred: 

“The language of human rights and its greatest crimes—apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc.—has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.” 

Segal doesn’t bother disputing the many well-evidenced allegations of apartheid, ethnic cleansing and genocide levelled at Israel. Nor does she consider that comparisons to the Nazis might diminish if Israel dismantled its concentration camps and Israeli politicians stopped quoting Hitler. Her report is remarkably devoid of any facts or engagement with arguments and counter-arguments. It reads like a News Corp opinion piece.

That’s because her primary objective is to dismiss criticism of Israel out of hand on the basis that it inevitably leads to anti-Jewish racism. While she concedes that criticism of Israel is not

inherently

antisemitic, she argues it is “utilised to create an environment where that sentiment can so easily morph into hostility towards Jewish people”. She terms this “ambient antisemitism”, which increases the danger of “conflation”, where “Jews in Australia are treated as collectively responsible for the actions of Israel”. 

There

is

 a danger that people disgusted by Israel’s actions misdirect their anger toward Jewish people as a whole. The Palestine solidarity movement has made every effort to combat this by distinguishing between Jewish people as a politically diverse religious and ethnic group on the one hand, and the state of Israel on the other. 

Segal, for her part, reinforces this conflation. It is laid out explicitly in her report: “Jewish identity is inherently linked to the land of Israel; it is central to the existence of Jewish people, the Jewish religion and culture”. This is echoed by Israeli politicians who cynically claim to represent the

entire Jewish community

 while committing unspeakable crimes. 

So far, these are the predictable arguments of the pro-Israel right. But as you dig deeper into the report, things get weirder. Segal thinks progressive antisemitism is dangerous not only because it legitimises criticism of Israel, but because it can act as a Trojan horse for more sinister ideologies.

Mainstream progressives are guilty, in her eyes, of “effectively laundering far-left antisemitism and Islamic extremism through a progressive lens … giving fundamentally extremist ideologies an apparently acceptable face”. 

Segal’s report makes repeated reference to this supposed intersection of radical-left politics and Islamic extremism, sanitised and promoted by respectable liberals. It is a wild conspiracy theory, one that sounds remarkably similar to Trump’s recent rants blaming rioting in France on an alliance of “migrants, jihadists, and communists”.

The language in her report mirrors that of right-wing intellectuals and government ministers overseas who rail against “Islamo-leftism”. This is the new iteration of the old myth of “Judeo-Bolshevism”, a …

author: Wendy Bacon, Cathy Peters
title: Time to reassess the antisemitism envoy’s role
content:
Civil liberties and Palestinian supporters are calling for the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, Jillian Segal, to be sacked after her latest report accused them of using “human rights” to hide their antisemitism.

Segal’s Plan to Combat Antisemitism appears designed to raise the pressure on all levels of government as well as the forthcoming final report of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion in December.

Segal is an active player in an international network, coordinated by key pro-Israel Jewish bodies as well as the United States State Department. Indeed, if it had not been for pressure from the US government, Segal might not have the job at all.

Segal is one of 32 Special Envoys in North America, Europe, South America, Israel and Australia.

The position of the US Special Envoy to Combat and Monitor Antisemitism was established in 2004, when New Jersey Republican congressman Chris Smith, who has a history of advocating for Israel and a record of accusing organisations including UN bodies of rampant antisemitism, successfully pushed to pass legislation creating the position.

Following the US lead, the European Union appointed an Envoy in 2015, followed by Canada, Greece, the Organization of American States and Britain. Israel’s envoy is part of its Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

In 2021, Smith, by then a strong supporter of Donald Trump, successfully pushed for an amendment which strengthened the position of US Special Envoy to the level of ambassador. They report directly to the Secretary of State, are appointed by the President and, crucially, can access foreign governments.

The ambassador’s mission is to promote US foreign policy by developing and implementing policies and projects to support action against antisemitism.

The office uses the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition, which directly links Jewish people with Zionism and the State of Israel, and conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism.

The current US Antisemitism Ambassador is far right winger Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun. He has boasted about influencing governments and recently described his office as supporting Trump’s policies by having 250,000 visas cancelled to keep campuses “‘safe”, interfering in foreign educational curricula and initiating prosecutions of what he describes as “hate crimes”.

This is echoed in Segal’s plan, which include compulsory training for Home Affairs staff responsible for certain visa applications and a new task force to review existing visas.

While it was initially reluctant, the Anthony Albanese Labor government appointed Segal in July 2024, after intense lobbying from the US State Department, which the Australian media did not cover.

FOI releases show that in May 2024, Aaron Keyek, the then US deputy antisemitism envoy, met with Australian officials in Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Attorney General’s Department to pressure the Albanese government to appoint an envoy.

Keyek also met with Deborah O’Neill, the Co-Chair of Labor Friends of Israel.

The crunch came with an ultimatum regarding a meeting of special envoys in Argentina, in July 2024, to sign US-drafted global guidelines to counter antisemitism.

A former senior US official told Jerusalem News Syndicate: “We were all diplomatic about it, but we told Australia, essentially, ‘It’s going to be glaring’. We didn’t want to repeat the situation, where one of our closest allies didn’t stand up to one of the top foreign-policy priorities when it comes to human rights that the United States is pushing internationally… So we told them that they could only attend if the delegation was led by a special envoy.”

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sent a cable to the US State Department on July 4 advising of the imminent appointment of an envoy who would report directly to the Prime Minister.

Segal was appointed on July 9, just 10 days before the meeting in Buenos Aires, which she attended. According to that cable, she had already approved the guidelines and her tickets had been booked before she was appointed.

Australia’s Ambassador to Argentina was permitted to sign off on the guidelines which refer to the IHRA definition as a key tool for fighting antisemitism, as a result of Segal’s hasty appointment.

In 2019 the New York based World Jewish Congress (WJC), the central governing organisation of Jewish organisations, which “defends the Jewish state of Israel”, established the Special …

author: Liza Stephens
title: Students strike against Hanson
content:
For the third time this year, thousands of high school students across the country walked out of class on 12 November to reject One Nation’s far-right agenda. Buoyed by the youth revolt igniting Europe, the protesters drew direct links between their fight and the one against our own monsters here in Australia. 

Students faced a deluge of condescending articles in the media decrying the long-term developmental dangers of missing an afternoon of classes. Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek suggested it was just an excuse for students to wag school, "We'll see how many kids turn up if it's a Saturday”. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said, “These kids really need to get back to class”.

Students proudly clapped back though creative handmade signs which read: “We are skipping class to teach you a lesson” and “The only minority destroying Australia is the rich”. In Sydney, protesters were cheered on by workers at a construction site as they made their way through the CBD.

“Migrants are welcome, Hanson is not” was a popular chant, an expression of solidarity between the protesters and their migrant classmates who are facing the brunt of One Nation’s extreme racism. Minh, a Vietnamese university student speaking at the Adelaide rally, pointed out Labor’s complicity in the increasingly right-wing climate:

“Labor’s tripling of student visa fees and the barring of international student family members is an attack on the rights of migrants. These cowards are happy to appease Hanson while punching down on the rest of us.”

References to the courageous student movements overseas were met with huge cheers. Australian young people connect with the problems driving students in Europe to protest, including having their futures sold off to the highest bidder, the racist politicians who legitimise genocide and then speak down to young people who call them out, and the schools left under-funded while governments hand tax cuts to the rich and billions to the military.

Luca, a high school speaker in Brisbane, spoke to the sentiment underpinning the protests: 

“I refuse to sit and accept the terror inflicted all across the planet by the minority ruling class. We must rise up and join France, Spain, Germany, Serbia and many more in their fight. We all have the same goal, and we can only win if we move together.”

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Protesters condemn state government attacks on Palestine solidarity, free speech
content:
Rallies were held across the country on November 15 to express solidarity with the people of Palestine and oppose repression of speech and protest by all levels of government.

The national day of action against repressive laws was called by Justice for Palestine Magan-djin (JFP) as part of its campaign to repeal the Queensland Liberal National Party government’s laws which criminalise Palestine solidarity slogans including “From the river to the sea” and “Globalise the intifada [uprising]”.

Chris Minns’ NSW Labor government is supporting the Queensland LNP government in the High Court challenge brought by JFP to overturn the laws. Victorian Liberals leader Jess Wilson has vowed to ban the phrase “Globalise the intifada” if elected on November 28.

JFP spokesperson Remah Naji said repression is “uniting our political class” and “thousands of us are united in defending our right to protest genocide”.

“The crimes remain the crime of genocide, the crime of occupation and the crime of apartheid. There is no amount of repression that will distract us from Israel’s crimes or absolve our government from its complicity in them.”

Michael Bradley, from MARQUE Lawyers, which is representing JFP in the High Court Case, said: “Queensland is currently leading the way with its ridiculous law that criminalises mere words, but other states are watching and keen to follow suit.

“It is more critical than ever that a stand is taken — in the courts and on the street — to demand our basic rights: to assemble, to protest and to speak.”

The crack down comes as Israel continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza and the Occupied West Bank, despite the so-called ceasefire. Its strike on the Nasser Hospital on November 12 — the only functioning hospital in Gaza — which killed six people, including surgeon Dr Rizq Shaira and a teenage patient, was condemned by 18 countries for violating international law.

As winter floods, storms and cold descend, many are still left sheltering in tents because of Israel’s restriction of supplies into Gaza. A nine-month-old baby died from hypothermia in Khan Younis in Southern Gaza on November 12 due to exposure to extreme cold.

Israel has killed at least 1610 Palestinians since the so-called ceasefire took effect.

Jonathan Strauss reports that 500 people marched in Magan-djin/Brisbane behind a large banner featuring the banned slogan “From the river to the sea”, a frequent chant of the Palestine solidarity movement.

The other banned slogan, “Globalise the intifada”, was not commonly used at Palestine rallies in Magan-djin, but expresses a desire for international support for the Palestinian people.

Anti-Zionist Jewish activist Stephen Heydt told the crowd that “kifah” means “fight” in Arabic. At the end of his speech he and others revealed t-shirts with the “globalise” slogan.

Police soon forcefully intervened, arresting seven people throughout the rally, including Heydt and two women who had carried the lead banner.

Naji said genocide was the real crime, not protesting the complicty of the Queensland and federal government.

The seven arrests add to the 31 previously made under the anti-free speech laws. Some, like Heydt, have now been arrested twice.

JFP is pursuing a High Court challenge to strike down the anti-free speech laws. It is asking for financial support for this and is organising a fundraising event on December 11.

The rally also featured music from a local punk band and a Riff Raff brass contingent.

Pip Hinman reports from Gadigal Country/Sydney that hundreds took to the streets again for Gaza on November 15. They demanded that NSW and federal Labor take action for Palestine, and stop trying to suppress free speech — particularly those speaking up against genocide.

The protest was called to show solidarity with pro-Palestine supporters in Queensland, who are being criminalised for standing up against genocide, and called for the scrapping of bans on phrases which call for rights, dignity, peace and justice for those living between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.

Minns wants to bring in similar laws, but is waiting on the outcome of the High Court challenge.

Speakers at the protest included Dr Shamikh Badra, who is from Gaza. He called on the federal government to act for Palestine, and not allow the weapons trade to continue.

Badra condemned the strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza. He said people were still being denied food, medical assistance and other aid, and …

title: Government invokes ‘bullet costs’ but ignores workers in peace process
content:
The Ministry of Health's proposed budget for 2027 will be discussed by the Parliamentary Planning and Budget Committee today, Monday. Ahead of the discussions, Diren Can Kaya, a member of the Istanbul-Aksaray Branch Executive Board of the Health and Social Services Workers' Union (SES), spoke about the unequal distribution of budget allocations, the resources transferred to private capital through city hospitals and the problems facing healthcare workers.


Kaya highlighted inequalities in budget allocations, saying that a total of 3.3 trillion Turkish lira had been allocated to security and defence spending, while only 1 trillion 196.6 billion lira had been earmarked for healthcare. Kaya said that the budget deficit had reached 4.1 trillion lira and that a large proportion of the budget was being directed towards interest payments and security policies.


 


Even during the peace process, workers have not benefited from the budget


Kaya recalled that the government's response to their demand for “A budget for health and education, not war” in previous years had been to ask, “Do you know how much a bullet costs?” Referring to figures released by the Ministry of Treasury and Finance, Kaya emphasised the importance of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


Kaya said that the 40-year war had cost workers in Turkey 2.3 trillion dollars: “Figures released by the Ministry of Finance show that 2.3 trillion dollars came out of the pockets of workers in Turkey during the 40-year war. Despite nearly two years of discussions about democratic society and peace, we see that the current budget has brought no benefits to workers. Yet these resources could have been used to establish healthcare and community centres in cities, providing services in people's mother tongues, rather than being spent on security policies. Domestic peace can only be established through policies that benefit the people.”


Kaya also highlighted shortcomings in primary healthcare, saying that deficiencies in services designed to prevent illness and provide care for conditions that do not require hospitalisation must be addressed. Kaya also pointed to the barriers preventing sick prisoners from accessing healthcare and said that the budget should be structured to guarantee their right to treatment.


‘The current system creates artificially stimulated demand for healthcare’


Kaya said that while 1.5 trillion liras had been allocated to curative healthcare services, preventive healthcare had not received an adequate share of the budget. Criticising a budget policy focused on treating illnesses rather than preventing them, Kaya said: “What we have is not really a Ministry of Health budget, but rather a ‘Ministry of Illness’ budget. Looking at the budgets over the past three years, we see only minimal increases, with figures of 6.2, 6.9 and 7.2. However, as the Health and Social Services Workers' Union, we emphasise that the existing problems in healthcare cannot be resolved unless its share of the budget rises above 10 percent.”


Kaya also criticised the city hospital model, saying that resources allocated from the healthcare budget through the Build-Operate-Transfer model were being channelled to private capital and what Kaya described as “illness lobbies”.


Kaya said: “With the resources transferred to city hospitals, 300 new healthcare facilities with 600 beds each could have been established. Similarly, the budget allocated to city hospitals over 25 years could have been used to rebuild approximately 900 hospitals. The current system constantly directs people towards emergency departments and hospitals, creating ‘artificially stimulated demand for healthcare’. Patients are being deprived of their right to healthcare.”


‘There is a huge workforce waiting for healthcare appointments’


Kaya emphasised that doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers were not responsible for the failures of a healthcare system that produces illness rather than health. Kaya also acknowledged that the union had not done enough to explain this reality to the public. Kaya said that healthcare workers were among the lowest-paid public employees and that excessive workloads and duties imposed on them were causing serious burnout.


Kaya said, “There is a system that constantly directs people towards emergency departments and hospitals while undermining preventive healthcare,” and adding that health should be understood not merely in physical terms, but as a state of …
