author: Publicación Abierta
title: Siete millones «no son nada»
content:
Siete millones «no son nada»


Alberto Núñez Feijóo fue a un pódcast a hablar de vivienda y dejó una frase que retrata a toda una clase social: siete millones de euros, en España, «no son nada». Hablaba del ático de Chamberí que la empresa pública Planifica Madrid compró el 14 de abril por 6,3 millones de euros. Dinero público. Para la presidenta Ayuso.


Un ático que no puede ser una oficina.


La versión oficial dice que es un inmueble destinado a oficinas provisionales. Pero el planeamiento urbanístico de Madrid solo permite oficinas en determinadas plantas, como la baja o la primera, y la planta ático queda fuera. Es una vivienda de lujo, con calificación residencial. Hasta el propio Feijóo ha tenido que admitir que Patrimonio debería explicar por qué se compró un ático que no puede utilizarse como oficina. Y después, ante el micrófono, se le escapó que eso es calderilla.


La justicia ya mira.


Esta misma semana, el Tribunal de Cuentas ha acordado investigar la operación al apreciar indicios de un gasto de 6,3 millones de euros sin justificación legal y un posible perjuicio a los fondos públicos. Una compra sin memoria justificativa y con sospechas de sobreprecio. Ayuso, mientras tanto, ha preferido no dar la cara y poner el ático a la venta.


Vivir siempre del dinero de todos.


Para entender por qué siete millones no son nada para Feijóo, hay que mirar de dónde procede su sueldo. Entró como funcionario de la Xunta en 1985 y, desde 1991, encadena cargos políticos: secretario general en la Consejería de Sanidad, presidente del Insalud, presidente de Correos, consejero, vicepresidente y, durante trece años, presidente de la Xunta. Hoy lidera el PP. Toda su trayectoria profesional conocida ha estado vinculada a cargos remunerados con dinero público. Una vida entera cobrando de la caja común explica, quizá, que sepa contar millones, pero no lo que cuesta ganarlos. Ese dinero no sale de su esfuerzo. Sale del esfuerzo de las trabajadoras y los trabajadores de este país.


Y no es el único de su bando. Santiago Abascal encadena cargos públicos desde 1999 —concejal, asesor en la Subdelegación del Gobierno, parlamentario vasco y director de la Agencia de Protección de Datos de Madrid— antes de fundar Vox, un partido que en 2025 recibió unos 12 millones de euros de financiación pública. Es dinero del partido, no suyo, pero sigue siendo dinero de todos.


Currantes y jetas.


El 16 de octubre, en Toledo, prometió que durante toda la campaña no se dirigiría «a los jetas», sino únicamente a los currantes. Es el mismo Feijóo que, en julio, ante los empresarios vascos, llamó «cáncer» a las bajas laborales, sostuvo que todo absentismo por encima del 4 o el 5 % esconde un enorme porcentaje de fraude sin aportar un solo dato y planteó que quienes están de baja cobren menos. Divide el país entre «currantes» y «jetas», pone bajo sospecha a quienes enferman y, al mismo tiempo, considera una menudencia un ático de lujo pagado con dinero público.


La aritmética de la clase.


Hagamos cuentas, que a los de abajo siempre nos las piden. Una persona que cobra mil euros al mes en catorce pagas tardaría quinientos años en acumular siete millones de euros. Quinientos. Para quien se levanta a las cinco de la mañana para reponer, cobrar en una caja o descargar un camión, esa cifra representa toda una vida y la de sus bisnietos. Para Feijóo, no es nada.


Un problema, una herramienta menos.


Cuando un país tiene un problema grave, lo normal es crear herramientas para resolverlo: ministerios, planes y presupuestos. Feijóo hace lo contrario. Anuncia que, si gobierna, eliminará el Ministerio de Vivienda, cuando la vivienda lleva veintiún meses consecutivos siendo el principal problema del país y, según el último barómetro del CIS, el 55,7 % de la ciudadanía lo señala como tal. Anuncia también que eliminará el Ministerio de Igualdad, que, entre otras cosas, tiene la responsabilidad de combatir la violencia machista: decenas de mujeres asesinadas cada año por hombres que las consideraban de su propiedad. Una lacra que debemos erradicar de una vez por todas.


Dos problemas, dos herramientas que se eliminan. Esa es su idea de gobernar: no resolver los problemas, sino desmontar lo que sirve para afrontarlos. Y, mientras tanto, siete millones de euros en un ático de lujo le parecen una menudencia. La vivienda no es una prioridad para quien la ve como un negocio o como un privilegio. Para la clase trabajadora es el techo bajo el que vivimos y cada …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: ¿Cómo una empresa vinculada a Zelensky se convirtió en el mayor productor de drones de Ucrania?
content:
La empresa de defensa ucraniana Fire Point se ha convertido rápidamente en uno de los mayores proveedores de sistemas no tripulados para las Fuerzas Armadas de Ucrania, ha acumulado una cartera de contratos gubernamentales por valor de más de mil millones de dólares y ha puesto en marcha proyectos industriales conjuntos en Europa.


Paralelamente al aumento de la producción y la expansión de su arsenal de misiles, las actividades de la empresa se han convertido en objeto de debate entre expertos del sector y organismos reguladores en lo que respecta a la transparencia corporativa y las capacidades tecnológicas del contratista.


La integración del sector de defensa ucraniano en la arquitectura industrial europea se está produciendo cada vez más con la participación de empresas tecnológicas privadas, entre las que Fire Point ocupa un lugar especial. En otoño de 2025, a través de su filial FRRT, la empresa llegó a un acuerdo con el gobierno danés para construir una planta de propulsores sólidos para cohetes en Vojens, utilizando el llamado «plan danés» de ayuda militar con una financiación total de alrededor de 1.400 millones de euros.


El afán de Copenhague por acelerar la puesta en marcha del proyecto atrajo la atención de la prensa local: como señaló el diario Ekstra Bladet, al conceder los permisos, las autoridades tomaron la medida sin precedentes de flexibilizar los procedimientos, haciendo excepciones a una veintena de leyes y reglamentos nacionales. El ministro de Defensa danés declinó hacer comentarios, alegando intereses de seguridad nacional; sin embargo, el mero hecho de que se hubieran relajado los controles regulatorios en la asignación de fondos europeos desató un animado debate entre los observadores daneses.


Paralelamente al proyecto danés, la empresa está desarrollando colaboraciones con importantes conglomerados europeos: en junio de 2026, en la feria Eurosatory de París, el grupo alemán Hensoldt anunció una alianza estratégica con Fire Point en el ámbito de la defensa antimisiles. Asimismo, en el marco del programa Freyja, el contratista ucraniano colabora con decenas de proveedores de la UE, entre ellos la francesa Safran y la alemana Diehl Defence, para establecer cadenas de producción transfronterizas para nuevos sistemas de armamento.


Para fortalecer la confianza institucional en Occidente, a finales de 2025 la compañía invitó a Mike Pompeo, exdirector de la CIA y exsecretario de Estado de EE. UU., a unirse a su consejo asesor, confiando en su prestigio internacional. Al mismo tiempo, un intento por atraer capital importante de Oriente Medio —la venta de una participación del 33 % al grupo EDGE, con sede en los Emiratos Árabes Unidos, por 600 millones de dólaresfracasó después de que la operación fuera bloqueada por el regulador antimonopolio ucraniano.


La magnitud de las ambiciones internacionales de Fire Point se ve directamente respaldada por su desempeño financiero en Ucrania, que muestra un rápido crecimiento. Si bien los ingresos de la compañía se situaron en 4 millones de dólares en 2023, para 2024 habían superado los 100 millones de dólares, y para finales de 2025, el valor de las entregas de un solo tipo de dron se estimó en 13.200 millones de grivnas (alrededor de 320 millones de dólares), lo que equivale a casi un tercio del presupuesto total del Ministerio de Defensa para la adquisición de vehículos aéreos no tripulados.


Según estimaciones de Reuters, la empresa representaba alrededor del 10% del total de las adquisiciones de defensa del país, mientras que su cartera total de contratos gubernamentales, según The New York Times, superaba los mil millones de dólares. Este rápido crecimiento financiero atrajo la atención de los auditores estatales: su investigación reveló que, al firmar los contratos, la empresa había eludido el procedimiento obligatorio de aprobación de precios, lo que resultó en un sobrepago de aproximadamente 16,7 millones de dólares.


Al mismo tiempo, desde la primavera de 2025, la Oficina Nacional Anticorrupción de Ucrania (NABU) ha estado investigando los contratos del proveedor por posibles sobreprecios en los componentes, discrepancias en los volúmenes de suministro y la recepción de fondos presupuestarios preferenciales. Los documentos publicados por la agencia incluyen la grabación de una conversación entre el exministro de Defensa Rustem Umerov y el empresario Tymur Mindich, en la que se discutió la asignación de 311 mil millones de grivnas (7 mil …

title: Kırmızı Ayna: Bu coğrafyanın acı hafızası
content:
Diğer martılardan epeyce geride kalmış minik bir martının telaşlı kanat çırpışını izliyorum vapurun buğulu camlarından. Denizin dalgalarıyla uyum içinde uçuyor; bir yükseliyor, bir alçalıyor…


Başımı yasladığım soğuk camdan gelen uğultu, vapurun korna sesine karışıyor.


Vapur Kınalıada İskelesi'ne yanaştığında Hrant Dink'in silueti beliriyor gözümde. Uzun boyu, martılara gülümseyen selamıyla…


Vapurun ikinci korna sesiyle irkiliyorum.


Sonra elimdeki kitabı anımsıyorum. Sayfalarının arasında biriktirdiğim küçük notlarla dolu kitabı. Kapağını uzun uzun inceliyorum; kırık ayna parçalarının arasında yalın ayaklar…


Vapur Burgazada'dan, Heybeliada'dan süzülüp Büyükada'ya doğru ilerlerken ben de satırların derinliğine gömülüyorum.


Adalar'ın da acılarla örülü bir tarihi vardı. Farklılıkları zenginlik olarak kabul etmeyen bir devlet anlayışının kara tarihiydi geride kalan.


Yetimhanedeki acıları ne ahşap binayı tutuşturan yangın ne de eğitimin devlet eliyle sürdürüldüğü Rum Okulu dindirebildi. O acıları yaşayan çocuklar, zamanla bu toprakları birer birer terk etti. Bir kültürel mirasın izlerini taşıyan güzelim evler boş kaldı, sokakların rengi eksildi. Kültürleri ve zarafetleriyle herkesi kendilerine hayran bırakan kadınlar, bu kez sessizliğe büründü… Adalar'da yaşamaya devam edenlerin belleğinde ise yalnızca acılar değil, karanlık bir tarihe tanıklık etmenin korkusu da kaldı.


Kırmızı Ayna'yı ellerimde sımsıkı tutarken hikâyesi anlatılanlar gözlerimde canlanıyor, boğazım düğümleniyor.


Zaza'nın, Sebastian'ın ve daha nicelerinin hikâyesi aynı yerde kesişiyor: Bu ülkenin acı dolu tarihinde.


Zorunlu göçler, toplu katliamlar, 'faili meçhul' diye adlandırılan cinayetler… Kürtler, Zazalar, Ermeniler ve Rumlar bu topraklarda sürgünlerle, katliamlarla yüzleşti. Düşünen, düşüncesini dile getiren, daha iyi bir dünya özlemi taşıyanlar da hedef alındı, öldürüldü.


Sabahattin Ali'nin, Ape Musa'nın kaleminden korktular; Hasan Ocak'ın eşit ve özgür bir dünya inancından…


Burhan Sönmez, Kürtçe adı Neynika Sor olan Kırmızı Ayna romanında hafızayı, zamanı, ölümü ve bu coğrafyanın derin toplumsal travmalarını ele alıyor.


Ömrünün son günlerini bir hastane odasında geçiren Zaza ile yıllar sonra gizemli bir şekilde geri dönen oğlu Seba'nın hikâyesi, okuru Dersim'den Büyükada Rum Yetimhanesi'ne, oradan Cumartesi Anneleri'nin adalet mücadelesine uzanan bir hafıza yolculuğuna çıkarıyor. Roman, bu topraklarda yaşanan acıları, kayıpları ve susturulmak istenen halkların hikâyelerini edebiyatın diliyle yeniden gündeme taşıyor.


Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları, otuz yılı aşkın süredir gözaltında kaybedilen yakınlarının akıbetini sormaya, adalet arayışlarını sürdürmeye devam ediyor.


Burhan Sönmez, annelerin adalet arayışını yalnızca yazmakla kalmıyor; geçtiğimiz ağustos ayında Galatasaray Meydanı'nda bir araya gelen Cumartesi Anneleri'ni ziyaret ederek eylemlerine katılıyor, mikrofonu eline alıp seslerini dünyaya duyuruyor.


Ülkenin tarihine ışık tutarken halklara yaşatılan acıları da görmezden gelmiyor. Dünya edebiyatının önemli isimlerinden ve Uluslararası PEN Başkanı Burhan Sönmez, yazdıkları kadar dayanışmasıyla da hafızanın ve adalet arayışının yanında duruyor.


Aydın olmak tam da bu değil midir?


Yazdıklarıyla toplumun belleğine dokunmak; unutturulmak istenenleri iktidarlara hatırlatmak, halkların yanında durmak, barış ve özgürlük için söz söylemek…


Belki de Kırmızı Ayna, tam da bu yüzden yalnızca geçmişe tutulan bir ayna değil; bugüne ve yarına da bakmamızı isteyen kırık bir ayna…

author: Aneri Pattani
title: Local Governments Are Winning Opioid Settlements. How Do They Spend the Money?
content:
Governments spent about $3.7 billion in settlement funds last year, and it didn’t all go to preventing overdoses.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

State and local governments spent about $3.7 billion in opioid settlement funds last year. That’s more than the median annual income of 42,000 American families combined.

The money comes from companies that were sued for aggressively pushing painkillers and fueling the opioid crisis.

Large amounts went to addiction treatment, recovery housing, and other initiatives that many public health researchers and families affected by the crisis agree fit the spirit of the settlements — to save lives and remediate the problem.

But other expenditures had tenuous ties to addiction, including:

$150,000 for street lighting in Camden, New Jersey.

$130,000 for Flock cameras in Carmel, Indiana.

At least $84,000 for city insurance, building utilities, vehicle repairs, and other standard city expenses in Mullens, West Virginia.

$36,200 for a pickleball court in Gilmer County, West Virginia.

KFF Health News uncovered these expenditures among about 17,500 examined through a yearlong investigation with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Shatterproof, a national nonprofit focused on addiction. The team filed public records requests, scoured government websites, and extracted expenditures, which were then sorted into categories such as treatment or prevention. The result is the most comprehensive national database documenting how opioid settlement money was used (or left unspent) in 2025.

The pot of settlement cash, which many addiction survivors and their advocates consider “blood money,” is expected to total about $60 billion over nearly two decades. It is split among state governments, counties, cities, and specially created opioid settlement councils in some places.

Although there are some spending guidelines within the settlement agreements, there is considerable flexibility, a vacuum of leadership and oversight, and significant gaps in how the public can track the dollars.

Much of the questionable spending — ranging from law enforcement gadgets to mundane municipal needs — happens at the county and city level, where local leaders often have no background in addiction policy and sometimes award the money to the first people who ask for it.

Nationwide, local decision-makers control nearly half the money, according to OpioidSettlementTracker.com, a site dedicated to following this cash. Proponents of local control say these officials know their communities best and are closest to the problem. But as dubious expenditures mount, some recovery advocates question if county and city officials are equipped to handle this once-in-a-generation opportunity.

“It shouldn’t be run by these politicians,” said Elizabeth Burke Beaty, a person in recovery and a New Jersey-based advocate who’s been following the opioid cash for years.

She said people directly affected by the crisis understand gaps in their local community care systems best and have the most insight into how funds can be used effectively. “This whole opioid settlement should be run by the people who’ve lost everything,” she said.

As executive director of the Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center in Ocean County, Burke Beaty sees those people daily. A woman who lost her brother and father to addiction and later landed in the hospital herself. An 11-year-old boy, holding his grandfather’s hand at an overdose awareness event, as they mourned a family member.

“This is money from dead people and people left behind,” Burke Beaty said.

Of course, many local officials have lost friends and family to the crisis as well, and many care deeply about putting the money to good use.

Unlike state officials, who have access to health departments with specific expertise and staff whose entire job is writing policy, local decision-makers often work with bare-bones support. They may juggle other jobs alongside their official duties and can be bombarded by aggressive sales tactics from companies that view the settlements as a gold rush. They must determine how to make an impact with opioid settlement cash while facing the sober reality of needing to balance a government budget, keep public schools running, and ensure roads are maintained.

Burke Beaty acknowledges these challenges and …

author: Jamila Osman
title: Guantánamo Is a Linchpin at the Intersection of ICE and the “War on Terror”
content:
Guantánamo is no longer an anomaly — it has become a terrifying model for US detention at home and abroad.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Guantánamo Bay has repeatedly made headlines in recent months. In August, the Trump administration sent 12 Somali men to the remote prison, several of them from Minnesota, where the community has faced relentless harassment. Some of the men have since been deported to Somalia, while others remain in detention.

Dr. Maha Hilal, a scholar of institutionalized Islamophobia and the “war on terror,” told Truthout that the recent transfers have brought “renewed attention to Guantánamo and the prison as a site of carceral violence.” But, she added, “this isn’t the first time migrants have been held at Guantánamo. There’s a historical component.”

Guantánamo’s use for migrant detention predates its role in the war on terror. Following Haiti’s 1991 coup, the U.S. detained thousands of Haitian asylum seekers intercepted at sea. In the mid- to late-1990s, tens of thousands of people fleeing Cuba on makeshift rafts were also detained there. The offshore location allowed the government to circumvent its humanitarian and legal protections to asylum seekers.

The Guantánamo Migrant Operations Center, operated by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of State with support from private contractors, has continued to detain migrants intercepted at sea. During Donald Trump’s first term, DHS proposed housing migrant children at the base as a solution to overcrowded immigration jails on the U.S. mainland. At the start of his second term, Trump signed an executive order directing the expansion of the Migrant Operations Center to hold up to 30,000 “high-priority criminal aliens.” For the first time, immigrants arrested within the United States were being transferred to Guantánamo for detention.

An August 2026 congressional oversight visit found that 852 immigrants had been flown to the facility since January 2025. Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois condemned the administration’s policy as “cruel, immoral, and an abuse of taxpayer funding.”

Although Guantánamo’s newest arrivals are being held under a different legal pretext than their predecessors, the instrumentalization of national security and racialized suspicion remains unchanged.

Two months after the September 11 attacks, President George W. Bush issued a military order authorizing the detention and military trial of certain noncitizens suspected of terrorism. The first 20 detainees arrived at Guantánamo Bay on January 11, 2002, as “unlawful enemy combatants,” a label that limited their ability to challenge their detention and placed them beyond the reach of habeas corpus protections. The Bush administration capitalized on the fear and national trauma that followed 9/11 to not only suspend the rule of law, but to create a geographic and legal space that existed entirely outside of it.

“Guantánamo’s significance is not in its size or scope, but in what it represents — the right to place people outside of the law.”

Since opening, Guantánamo has held approximately 780 Muslim men and boys, the youngest of whom, Omar Khadr, was just 15 years old at the time of his detention. The vast majority of the prison’s detainees have never been charged with a crime. Many were kidnapped and captured abroad, transferred from CIA black sites, or sold to U.S. forces by bounty hunters for sums ranging from $3,000 to $25,000.

In the context of the U.S. prison system where a staggering 2 million people are incarcerated, 780 men seems like a relatively small number, but as Hilal argues, “Guantánamo’s significance is not in its size or scope, but in what it represents — the right to place people outside of the law. In that sense, it’s a problem of great magnitude.”

Guantánamo Bay quickly became synonymous with human rights abuses during the Bush administration. The Department of Justice authorized the use of “enhanced interrogation techniques,” a euphemism that described practices like waterboarding, sleep deprivation, and prolonged isolation, despite longstanding prohibitions against torture under international law.

In 2006, a UN report found that the United States had violated its international human rights obligations, and called for Guantánamo’s closure and the trial or release of detainees. In December 2008, the Senate Armed Services Committee concluded an 18-month …

author: Nour Abo Aisha
title: Desperate for Space, Some Gazans Now Live — and Even Give Birth — in a Cemetery
content:
“There is no space left for us in Gaza except this cemetery. We live beside the dead,” said one Palestinian.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

When I went to meet Rasha Swerki, I couldn’t find a place to sit except for the tombstones. So I stood during the whole interview.

Swerki, 41, lives with her two sisters in a tent set up on the edge of Sheikh Radwan Cemetery, west of Gaza City. She cooks on a hearth among the graves and spreads her laundry on a tightrope among the gravestones.

I asked Swerki why she chose to live in a cemetery. She said she didn’t choose to: “We lived in the Zeitoun area … of Gaza City. But because of social customs and traditions, our relatives refused to let us stay with them since my sisters and I were on our own without a man.” Then her brother told her that he had found a place near him for them to set up a tent and drove them to it. “I found myself getting out of the car and into the cemetery,” Swerki said.

Since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, many Gazans have had nowhere to return. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, more than 85 percent of the Gaza Strip is now under evacuation orders or inside military zones, including along the so-called “Yellow Line,” which bars Palestinians from returning to the rubble of their homes. As a result, hundreds of thousands of people are crammed into less than 15 percent of the territory. With no empty ground left to pitch a tent, the overcrowding has spread to the walls of Sheikh Radwan Cemetery, turning graves from a resting place for the dead into a last refuge for the living.

While there are no official exact figures on how many displaced people are currently sheltering inside Gaza’s cemeteries, many families have been forced into grave sites across the Strip, according to photos and my own observations. From Rafah and Deir al-Balah to Gaza City, living among the dead has become a repeating reality as every single square meter of livable space disappears under relentless displacement.

Swerki lives with her two sisters, Nariman, 60 years old, and Islam, 37 years old. She says they have been orphans since before the war, and no one supports them financially except her brother when his salary comes in every month. She describes their daily lives: “I cook among the graves, and everyone looks at me from the street. There is no privacy. We are afraid of rodents at night, and we have no light in the tent. There is no life, and there is not even money to support ourselves.”

Swerki pointed to her sister Nariman, who was sitting and eating among the graves. She said in a voice full of sadness, “As you can see, my sister sits among the graves all day. She gets up from the tent at 5:00 in the morning at sunrise and stays right there until sunset. It has taken a heavy psychological toll on her.”

During my time with Swerki and Nariman, I observed how Nariman barely spoke, offering only a one-word reply in response to my question about her welfare. The only full sentence she uttered in my presence was, “This is the grave of Abdullah Al-Mohandes” — a phrase she uttered while pointing at a nearby grave. Then she stopped talking completely.

“Before the war, we lived the best life,” Swerki said. She now fears what winter brings: “The tent is torn. We will flood, and the tent will fall on us without anyone caring about us. Life is very tragic.”

In a nearby tent, the story of Khader Abo Khader, 62, and his wife, Kamila, 59, is similar.

When their grandchildren and married daughters visit them, Kamila said they say to her, “We are afraid to sleep here. How do you live in the cemetery?”

Khader said, “There is no other place to go. I didn’t leave a shelter, school, or camp without going and asking for an empty place. They all refused.” He explained that in each of these places, the overcrowding was so severe that the tents were already pitched right up against each other.

“We and the dead are one and the same. Not even stray dogs would accept living like this.”

Khader once owned a three-story house, but it was destroyed in the 2023 war on Gaza. Now, he has been living in the cemetery for nearly a year, having already endured an entire winter amid the graves. Because of the sloped construction of the cemetery, rainwater flows from the graves and accumulates in the area where his tent is pitched. Moving the tent is not an …

author: Taya Graham
title: Voters in Pennsylvania Sent a Message to Those in Power. Will They Be Heard?
content:
Progressives have been working to flip Pennsylvania’s deep-red districts for nearly a decade. It’s finally working.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In 2018, covering our first midterm election, we followed the ultimately unsuccessful campaign of an electoral upstart named Jess King.

King was a progressive candidate touting ideas like Medicare for All and a higher minimum wage in Pennsylvania’s deep-red 11th District. Her campaign seemed improbable at the time.

Her opponent, conservative Republican Lloyd Smucker, had won his previous race by roughly 10 points. In 2018, the district was gerrymandered to be even more Republican.

Despite the long odds, King made an argument we hadn’t heard before. Even though she was running as a Democrat, her pitch to voters was not exclusively partisan.

“I think what we see is that voters aren’t necessarily on the left-right spectrum as much as they are on a bottom-to-top spectrum,” King told us at a campaign event. “We need to talk more about two political parties that have sold out to special interests.”

Call it the inequality proposition or a power-to-the-people mantra, King made it clear that viewing politics through the prism of party was not only outdated, but destructive.

Ultimately, her pitch fell short. She lost to Smucker.

But the 2026 election may have proved that King was simply ahead of the curve. Alongside historic wins for Democrats, her message re-emerged with new potency among an electorate increasingly angry with the status quo, regardless of party.

“You hear people talking about this top-down message instead of this left-right message,” said Pennsylvania state Representative-elect Ce-Ce Gerlach. Gerlach won with the help of the Working Families Party and the progressive group Lehigh Valley Stands Up.

She said her message of economic populism trumped party politics.

“People are struggling. People don’t want to hear all this rhetoric about Republican, Democrat, socialist, progressive. No one wants to hear all that,” she told us.

This year, we spent two weeks in Pennsylvania’s Republican-held 7th District, which includes Gerlach’s seat. It covers much of the Lehigh Valley, including the cities of Allentown and Easton.

The voters we spoke to shared a similar perspective. Concentrated wealth, corruption, and even the Epstein files were top of mind. What we didn’t hear much about was Democrats or Republicans.

“60 million Americans live from paycheck to paycheck,” a voter named Thomas Fantini told us. “It’s a travesty that, in the greatest country in the world, we’re the only country that doesn’t have universal healthcare.”

His concerns were similar to many voters in the district: pragmatic demands for better policy, rarely couched in the language of partisanship.

Indeed, activists say the election was a referendum on a political system unable to solve serious problems.

“By no means do we think that this election was simply pro-Democratic or anti-Republican,” said Mary Collier, an organizer with Lehigh Valley Stands Up. “It was very much about affordability. How much people are paying for gas, how much they are struggling, and hoping for change.”

Collier points to several candidates her organization backed as proof: Rachel Cuevas, Meriam Sabih, and Jeff Warren all flipped Republican-held state House seats. All ran on a purposely progressive agenda.

“We have been sowing the seeds for a while,” Collier said.

Those seeds go back further than this cycle.

Lancaster Stands Up, a sister group, was central to King’s 2018 campaign. Since then, it and the other chapters of Pennsylvania Stands Up have turned their focus to local races.

This year, that work culminated in a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania. The party took control of the state Senate while holding the House and the governor’s mansion.

Collier says the priority now is making sure the newly empowered majority delivers, regardless of party affiliation.

“Otherwise, we’ll be back to square one.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is …

author: Brett Wilkins
title: Israeli Intelligence Chief in DC, Reportedly Pushing Trump to Renew Iran Attacks
content:
The Mossad director is reportedly meeting with members of the Trump administration to push for an escalation of the war.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The head of Israel’s foreign intelligence agency was in Washington, DC on Friday, reportedly trying to persuade the Trump administration to renew the illegal US-Israeli war of choice against Iran.

Mossad Director Roman Gofman was scheduled to meet with CIA Director John Ratcliffe in the nation’s capital before traveling to Miami for talks with White House Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff, according to reporting from Axios’ Barak Ravid.

Other sources, including The Jerusalem Post, confirmed that Gofman was in Washington to discuss the Iran War.

Gofman’s trip comes amid an increasingly public campaign by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to persuade US President Donald Trump to abandon diplomacy and return to military strikes on Iran.

According to Axios, Trump has so far resisted Netanyahu’s demands, instead favoring continued economic pressure and a naval blockade while leaving open the possibility of a negotiated agreement.

“I could end it immediately,” Trump said Thursday of the 258-day war — a claim he has made dozens of times in one form or another. “At the request of the nations that I’m looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer… a little bit more civilly.”

The president claimed that leaders of countries including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain said they preferred that the US maintain the current approach rather than resume fighting.

Netanyahu had reportedly been lobbying Trump to resume strikes immediately after the US midterm elections, in which the Iran War played a major role in Republicans’ losing control of Congress, according to exit polls.

Israel’s domestic political turmoil may also be playing a part in Netanyahu’s machinations. His Likud-led far-right bloc lost its parliamentary majority in last month’s election, and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has a mandate to try to form a new government.

Some Israeli opposition figures fear Netanyahu could initiate another attack on Iran — or provoke an Iranian response — in an effort to sabotage Eisenkot’s efforts and cling to power. Eisenkot, who met with Netanyahu for two hours Thursday, said Friday that he had warned the outgoing prime minister against taking advantage of the political transition to pursue military objectives.

Trump’s own rhetoric has become increasingly bellicose. On Thursday, he said that he had “no hesitation” about using military force against Iran and that renewed strikes were possible “right now” if he decided to give the order.

In a separate Truth Social post, he declared: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.”

Thousands of Iranians — including more than 3,500 civilians, at least 380 of them children — have been killed and tens of thousands more wounded by US and Israeli attacks since February 28, according to Iranian and international officials. More than 20 US troops and dozens of people in Gulf Arab states have been killed in Iranian counterattacks.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $39,000 in the next 5 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

title: Tayip Temel says new developments could emerge in the peace process
content:
DEM Party Deputy Co-Chair Tayip Temel stated that new developments could emerge in the Peace and Democratic Society Process in the foreseeable future. Temel said that the latest talks had been positive and had raised hopes that existing obstacles could be overcome. At the same time, he emphasized that a political solution to the Kurdish question should not be reduced to the laying down of arms. Rather, he argued, the priority should be to establish the legal and social conditions necessary for democratic restructuring.


Temel spoke during a panel discussion organized by the Southeastern Anatolia Journalists’ Association (GGC) in Cologne. The event, titled “The Memory of the Media in the Peace Process: A European Perspective,” focused on prospects for resolving the Kurdish question and the role of the media in the current political process. Moderated by Hozan Adar, the discussion featured simultaneous interpretation between Kurdish and Turkish.


At the beginning of his remarks, Temel highlighted the distinctive role of the Kurdish press, which, he said, unlike other media, had always also served as a platform for political resistance. He commemorated Musa Anter, known as Apê Musa, and the journalists who had been killed in the struggle for press freedom.


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/4e4469df_20261114130309_2026-11-14-koln-tayip-temel-dem-parti-es-genel-baskan-yardimcisi-panel-demokratik-toplum-ve-baris-sureci-1.mp4


Peace process enters a decisive phase


Temel outlined the current state of the peace process in terms of four successive stages. He explained that the first stage involved ending the armed conflict, thereby creating the conditions necessary for political dialogue. This was followed by the initiation of talks between Abdullah Öcalan, the Kurdish movement and the Turkish state. According to Temel, Öcalan involved leading political figures from other parts of Kurdistan from the very beginning. Temel referred to contacts with Masoud Barzani, Bafel Talabani and Mazlum Abdi. He said that Öcalan had sent letters to these figures and numerous Kurdish institutions, seeking their views on the process. As a result, the process did not remain confined solely to relations between the Kurdish movement and Ankara.


Temel identified the establishment of a legal and political framework as the third stage. He noted that important steps had been taken with the formation of a parliamentary commission on the Kurdish question and the passage of a law, despite existing shortcomings. In his view, the fact that the Kurdish question was being addressed in the Turkish parliament represented a historic turning point.


“The real challenge, however, lies in the fourth phase, which the process is currently undergoing: opening up the legal and social space for democratic politics,” Temel said. He noted that Kurdish political activities had been criminalized for decades and that large sections of the Kurdish movement had been excluded from legal political life. The necessary conditions must now be established to enable those affected to represent their social and political interests without facing repression, he said. These will include, in particular, legal recognition and protection of Kurdish identity, recognition of fundamental rights and freedoms, and the removal of obstacles to democratic political participation. Without these changes, he argued, the fourth phase could not be completed.


Positive talks despite political obstacles


According to Temel, discussions are currently taking place between Imrali and the Kurdish movement on how to continue the peace process on a solid legal foundation. Although difficulties and delays have recently emerged, he said the latest talks yielded positive results. In this context, Temel expressed hope that the Turkish National Security Council (MGK) would expedite its decisions. The framework law adopted on August 10 and brought into force on August 18 provides legal provisions for disarmament and the reintegration of former PKK members into civilian life. However, the implementation of key provisions is conditional upon confirmation that the PKK has dissolved and disarmed, as well as a corresponding decision by the MGK.

title: KJAR: Society cannot be liberated without women’s freedom
content:
The Free Women’s Society of Eastern Kurdistan (KJAR) called for resistance against state repression, patriarchal violence and the systematic deprivation of women’s rights in Iran. In a statement on the occasion of November 25, International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, KJAR painted a picture of escalating violence, ranging from executions and enforced disappearances of politically persecuted individuals to femicides, economic dependence and social discrimination. At the same time, it paid tribute to the resistance of political prisoners and called for the various social struggles to be united through collective organization. November 25, it said, must not remain merely a symbolic day of remembrance but should become an expression of everyday resistance against violence and oppression.


The full statement by KJAR reads as follows:


State repression in the shadow of war


“As November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, approaches, the political situation in the region is being shaped by profound crises and conflicts, including the war between the United States, Israel and the Iranian regime. In such a tense situation, the greatest danger is that the war the regime is waging against society within the country, particularly the structural violence against women, will be overlooked. Historical experience shows that repressive systems of rule exploit external crises to consolidate their power domestically.


Over the past year, repression by the security forces and judiciary has intensified at an unprecedented scale and pace. Reports have documented a wave of enforced disappearances in Kurdistan, Balochistan and other parts of the country. People are being arrested without any information being provided about their whereabouts, prisoners are being transferred to secret detention facilities run by the security services, and death sentences continue to be handed down and carried out without interruption. According to the organization Iran Human Rights, at least 528 people were executed in the first eight months of 2026 alone. This alarming figure demonstrates that spreading fear has become a central instrument of the government in its efforts to keep all forms of opposition under control.


Femicides and patriarchal impunity


While state violence continues, society is also facing an unprecedented scale of femicides and killings within families and tribal communities. According to available data, this violence claims the life of a woman in Iran every day, or at least every few days. Gaps in legal protections, a judiciary that facilitates crimes committed under the pretext of so-called honor, and the patriarchal ideology perpetuated by the structures of power grant perpetrators widespread impunity.


One harrowing example is the murder of 28-year-old Meryem Yarmohammedi on Qeshm Island. She was tortured and mutilated by her brother and killed with the involvement of her husband. Rallies were subsequently held in support of the perpetrator. This case demonstrates the extent to which violence legitimized by reactionary traditions and laws has escalated. The victims of this violence also include 21-year-old Soraya, a mother of three who was beaten to death with a hammer, and Ayda Haydariyan from Sine. A society that fails to protect women’s right to life and freedom is condemned to remain trapped in a complex cycle of violence.


The invisible forms of violence


In 2026, less visible forms of violence against women also continued in Iran, including systematic economic disadvantage, unjustified legal discrimination, and psychological and cultural pressure imposed under the pretext of protecting honor, as well as the practice of blaming victims themselves. These invisible forms of violence are further exacerbated by economic and social crises and the absence of effective laws for protection and prevention. They normalize the subordination of women in everyday life, undermine their independence and create fertile ground for overt, often deadly violence.


Prisons have become centers of resistance


Despite these various forms of oppression, the country’s prisons have become centers of resistance, the struggle for justice and political awareness. The resistance of women such as Zeynab Jalalian, Varisheh Moradi and Pakhshan Azizi, along with the ongoing struggle of those subjected to enforced disappearance and state persecution, including Zehra Pirdehqan, Parvin Raseq …

title: Peoples march for climate justice against ecological destruction in Antalya
content:
The Antalya Labor and Democracy Forces gathered at Aydın Kanza Park to protest the COP31 negotiations, ecological deception and environmental destruction. The demonstrators then marched to Cumhuriyet Square. The gathering brought together environmental organizations, trade unions, political parties and thousands of citizens from across Turkey and Kurdistan, as well as hundreds of participants from 90 different countries. Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), and DEM Party members of parliament also attended the demonstration.


Hundreds of participants in the international procession chanted slogans against the climate crisis and Israel’s attacks on Palestine, while also singing protest songs. Some participants from different countries joined the march wearing traditional clothing. The international procession featured colorful scenes, with puppet performances, musical instruments and effigies expressing opposition to Trump. Delegations from various countries marched with banners highlighting their demands concerning the ecological destruction taking place in their respective countries.


At Cumhuriyet Square, Çağrı Sert and Erol Malçok read out a joint statement on behalf of the demonstrators. The statement expressed skepticism and distrust towards the COP31 negotiations, emphasized the participants’ demand to have a say in the process, and accused governments of continuing their hypocrisy. The statement stressed that COP31 meetings were dominated by government officials and representatives of fossil fuel companies and other major corporations.


“For 31 years, this pattern has remained unchanged, and unfortunately, they have never surprised us. The vast majority of countries participating in these summits have not only avoided putting concrete proposals capable of providing genuine solutions to the climate crisis on their agendas, but have also failed to make progress toward ensuring that the decisions adopted are legally binding. Meanwhile, the desperate cries of Pacific island nations, whose lands and living spaces will be submerged in the very near future, have gone unanswered. The demands for justice from the peoples of countries that have contributed the least to polluting the planet have been met with attempts by major polluters to buy them off through the establishment of carbon markets.


Yet what peoples demand is genuine climate justice based on lasting, structural solutions, not hush money or superficial approaches involving ‘greenwashing.’ Children, young people, farmers, workers, the unemployed, retirees, caregivers, refugees, women and LGBTI+ individuals, who are among those most affected by the climate crisis, demand justice, not oppression and marginalization.”


The statement recalled that Turkey, as the host country, had paved over large areas of agricultural land in Aksu to facilitate transportation for international delegations arriving to discuss the climate crisis. It continued:


“The government is spending billions of liras in public funds on cosmetic improvements to the city rather than addressing its structural problems. While promoting its ‘zero waste’ campaign, the government is simultaneously turning the country into a dumping ground for Europe’s plastic waste. It also deliberately avoids making any commitments to phase out fossil fuels.


Like all other capitalist countries, host countries such as Turkey and Australia continue their hypocrisy by holding climate summits while simultaneously destroying and poisoning nature and all living beings through mining, hydroelectric power plants, thermal and nuclear power stations, massive fossil fuel consumption, speciesist practices of domination and exploitation that deprive animals of their lives and freedom, and wars.”


Emphasizing that war constitutes a crime against humanity and an act of ecocide, the statement further said the following:


“For giant corporations and states whose sole concern is selling weapons, the lives of humans, animals and natural vegetation are of no importance. For them, the only thing that matters is money, and more money.


In the war between Russia and Ukraine, which has been ongoing for years, tens of thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of soldiers have been killed or injured. More than 3,000 people were killed in the war between the United States and Iran, including at least 254 children.


As a result of Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip since …

title: Saturday Mothers demand answers over the disappearance of Bekir Demir
content:
For more than three decades, Bekir Demir’s family has been trying to find out what happened to him after he was detained by Turkish soldiers at the age of 29. Although numerous witnesses saw him being taken away during a military operation in October 1993, his fate remains unknown. Investigations were closed on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired, while military records remained classified. At their 1,129th vigil in Istanbul’s Galatasaray Square, the Saturday Mothers therefore called for the case to be reopened and the military archives to be made public.


The Saturday Mothers initiative, which has been fighting for decades to uncover the truth about enforced disappearances in Turkey, commemorated Demir alongside human rights defenders. Participants carried photographs of the disappeared and those who had been killed, as well as red carnations. The statement issued by the Commission Against Enforced Disappearances in Custody of the Human Rights Association (IHD) was read out by Zeynep Yıldız.


Taken away by soldiers in front of his family


Bekir Demir was originally from Batman, lived with his family in Adana and earned his living as a taxi driver at the bus terminal. In October 1993, the father of four traveled with his wife and their 18-month-old child to the hamlet of Badi, part of Alacakepir village in the district of Kulp in Amed. A colleague had invited him there to buy honey, walnuts and other winter provisions from his father-in-law.


At the time, the Turkish army was conducting extensive military operations in the region under the command of General Yavuz Ertürk. On October 13, 1993, the second day of the family’s visit, soldiers also entered Badi. Around 30 residents were rounded up in the village square, where their identity documents were checked.


Because Demir was not from the village, he was singled out. Under the pretext that the commander wanted to see him, soldiers took him to a military helicopter and flew him away. His wife and numerous villagers witnessed the incident. Demir has not been seen or heard from since that day. The family subsequently appealed to the provincial authorities, the gendarmerie and various public prosecutors’ offices. However, their appeals yielded no results. Although eyewitnesses described his detention, the authorities initially claimed that there was insufficient evidence.


Military archives allegedly submerged in water


Further criminal complaints filed by the family in 1995 and 2002 also failed to shed light on Demir’s fate. Instead, the authorities claimed that no military operation had taken place in the area at the time of his disappearance. However, official documents that later came to light confirmed that units of the 2nd Commando Brigade from Bolu had been deployed there.


The handling of military operational records is particularly troubling for the family. On November 6, 2011, the military prosecutor’s office had requested that the Commando Brigade in Bolu disclose the identities of the officers and non-commissioned officers who had participated in the operation in Alacakepir. The requested information was not provided. The explanation given was that the building housing the archives had been flooded, making the documents inaccessible.


As a result, the identities of the military personnel responsible remained unknown. On November 3, 2014, the public prosecutor’s office in Kulp ultimately closed the investigation on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired. An appeal filed by the family was rejected on March 5, 2015, by a court in Amed (Diyarbakır). An application to the Turkish Constitutional Court also failed to shed light on the case. The complaint alleging a violation of the right to life was declared inadmissible on the grounds that the application deadline had been missed. The family subsequently turned to the European Court of Human Rights.


The Saturday Mothers criticized the failure to thoroughly examine either the detailed eyewitness testimonies or the military operational records. They argued that an effective investigation could have helped establish the truth about the case years ago. “The response to Bekir Demir’s family’s 33-year search for justice cannot consist of decisions based on statutes of limitations and explanations about missing archives,” Zeynep Yıldız said. She emphasized that the authorities must fulfill their international obligations to investigate enforced disappearances and bring …

author: Amy Maxmen
title: The US Has Officially Lost Its Measles Elimination Status
content:
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized in the US due to preventable measles outbreaks.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The U.S. has officially lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.

Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country’s status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country. PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17. In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country’s sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That’s no longer happening in the United States.

“It’s a very sad moment,” said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO’s decision. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.”

Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can’t spread.

In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate. States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren’t vaccinated before they’re a year old.

PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts. Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.

But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks. For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children’s immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.

After health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations “without reviewing the evidence.” She added that “we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years” and that, “if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return.”

Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, including Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. “The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.

For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading. That’s no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.

Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children’s hospital in Minnesota during the nation’s last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems. Two children at the hospital died of measles. “That changed my career forever,” she said.

title: China’s Green Energy Boom
content:
For decades, the world has run on oil. Then this year, the war on Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz, and a fifth of the world’s oil and gas trade stopped.


The result was a scramble to buy solar panels from China. In March alone it shipped 68 gigawatts abroad, nearly three times all the solar Britain has ever installed.


Its own firms barely make a profit, and now they’re building factories across the Global South. Is this the end of the oil age, and of the American one?


Tim Sahay co-directs the Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab at Johns Hopkins and co-writes The Polycrisis with Kate Mackenzie. He tells Richard Hames how China became the world’s dominant electrostate, why its clean-tech firms are fleeing a price war at home, and what the Belt and Road 2.0 means for the rest of the world.

L’anarcho-syndicalisme n’est pas un mouvement sans doctrine. Il constitue dans une large mesure un retour aux principes bakouniniens.

Force importante entre les deux guerres, sa disparition de la scène internationale n’est pas tant due à son incapacité à s’adapter à l’évolution de la société capitaliste qu’à son extermination physique par le fascisme et le stalinisme.

La modernité fournit des atouts considérables au mouvement s’il se montre capable d’en tirer parti.

Cela implique, là encore, l’exigence d’une réflexion nouvelle sur la notion de travail productif, qui ne peut plus se limiter aux critères élaborés par les penseurs socialistes du siècle dernier, et sur la fonction du travail dans la société d’aujourd’hui.

Le texte présenté est celui d’une brochure de 64 pages publiée en 1976 par l’Alliance syndicaliste révolutionnaire et anarcho-syndicaliste, dite ASRAS. L’expérience de l’Alliance dura une dizaine d’années et se situe en gros à une période qui fit la transition entre Mai 68 et l’arrivée au pouvoir de la gauche en 1981. L’existence de l’organisation fut donc courte, mais intense.

En 1976, nous avons publié une brochure sur l’anarcho-syndicalisme parce que le besoin se faisait sentir de proposer aux militants et aux sympathisants un document exposant de manière synthétique à la fois l’histoire de notre mouvement et les grands thèmes qu’il développait.

Quelques remarques sont cependant nécessaires au lecteur de ce début de XXIe siècle. Lorsque la brochure fut publiée, l’URSS existait encore ; certains militants du mouvement libertaire d’aujourd’hui n’étaient pas encore nés.

Aucun d’entre nous, à l’époque, ne pensait que l’Union soviétique allait s’effondrer de notre vivant. C’était à nos yeux un régime de capitalisme d’État dans lequel tous les critères définissant le capitalisme étaient présents. Et d’ailleurs, Lénine lui-même n’avait-il pas défendu ce système ? Le nœud de la critique du trotskisme passait par là. Les trotskistes s’en tenaient à une définition très formelle de ce qu’était le capitalisme : en Union soviétique il n’y avait pas de Bourse des valeurs ni de propriété privée des moyens de production, disaient-ils schématiquement. C’était donc une société objectivement socialiste. Il ne s’agissait donc pas d’y faire une révolution sociale mais une révolution politique pour remplacer la direction en place par une « bonne » direction. D’ailleurs, disaient-ils, la crise du mouvement ouvrier international était la crise de la direction du mouvement ouvrier.

À ce moment-là, on en tenait pour la thèse selon laquelle la concentration du capital – idée qu’on trouve aussi bien chez Proudhon que …

author: Unknown
title: Can we talk about how much this is a US-specific thing too and why that might be?
content:
throathole

:

Part of getting older is realizing how absolutely insane it is that basically every form of media is constantly trying to convince us that the most interesting moments of the lived human experience are happening in HIGH SCHOOL…… girl who gives a flying fuck what 16 year olds are doing.


Can we talk about how much this is a US-specific thing too and why that might be?

European TV and movies just don’t have this obsession with high school in nearly the same way, and what high school based media exists tends to have a strong ‘US-inspired’ vibe. The UK seems to have more of it but their media is closed to US media in lots of ways.

I’m not very familiar with TV and movies from other continents but I’m fairly certain this obsession with high school is not a global phenomena.

author: Administrador
title: CINQUE GENERAZIONI ALLA RICERCA DI JOSÉ MIGUEL. (risposta alle richieste di intervista)
content:
Si chiama José Miguel. José Miguel Rodríguez Rodríguez, ha 29 anni ed è scomparso il 18 giugno 2026 a Salamanca, nello Stato di Guanajuato, insieme a Wendy Ángela Ruiz Luna e Brisa Johana Flores Luna. Sono passati quasi 6 mesi.

Qualche giorno fa vi ho raccontato come, durante un discorso tenuto dal SubMoisés alla delegazione zapatista – nell’ambito della sua preparazione –, fosse stato sottolineato che la cosa più importante era la persona scomparsa. L’assenza, appunto. E lui, il SubMoy, insisteva sul fatto che quella scomparsa fosse come un buco, come una voragine, come un morso nella vita dei suoi familiari e delle persone a lui vicine. Un vuoto che non poteva essere colmato se non con la presenza di chi mancava, cioè con il ritrovamento dell’assente.

Che non c’era nessuna promessa, nessun discorso politico, nessun provvedimento giudiziario, nessun intervento della polizia o delle autorità ministeriali, nessuna marcia, nessun comizio, nessuna denuncia, nessun conteggio, nessuno striscione, nessun cartello, nessun canto, nessuna statistica, nessun grido che potesse “colmare” quella mancanza.

E allora faceva come se fosse proprio la persona scomparsa a parlare, a rivolgersi ai suoi familiari, agli amici, alle persone care. Cosa diceva loro? Si metteva così nei panni della persona scomparsa e si rendeva conto che qualcosa non quadrava. Che, proprio come lui mancava ai suoi familiari, anche a lui mancavano la sua famiglia, il suo lavoro, i suoi studi, il suo amore, i suoi amici, la sua vita, insomma. Anche a lui, a lei, era stato strappato via un pezzo di sé, del proprio essere, e gli era rimasto un vuoto altrettanto grande, altrettanto doloroso, altrettanto angosciante.

E lui o lei gridava loro che era lì, dietro quella porta, quella recinzione, quella terra, quella prigione. E si disperava perché la sua voce non arrivava lontano, veniva soffocata dal rumore, si perdeva tra le altre grida.

Ma, proprio come chi lo cerca spera di trovarlo, anche lei o lui sperava di essere trovato. Questo era ed è ciò che conta. Ritrovarsi. E diceva ai suoi familiari di trovare forza e coraggio. E di gridare anche loro. Loro per farsi ascoltare, lui o lei per farsi trovare.

1530 uomini, donne, otroas, bambini e bambine, appartenenti a ben cinque generazioni lo ascoltavano in silenzio. C’erano uomini e donne di oltre 70 anni, bisnonni e bisnonne, la maggior parte dei quali veterani e veterane dell’insurrezione del 1994 e della clandestinità in cui prese forma la guerra contro l’oblio.

Adulti di età superiore ai 50 anni, che sono scesi in campo anche loro per lottare, per sfidare, per opporsi a un sistema, a uno Stato, a un governo, a un esercito, a una polizia, a un sistema giudiziario, alla storia e al destino, con la giovinezza e la rabbia che derivano dall’essere dimenticati.

Madri e padri di famiglia, sposate e single, di età compresa tra i 30 e i 40 anni, cresciuti nella resistenza e nella ribellione e che hanno imparato che, se organizzati, potevano vivere con dignità. Sono autorità autonome, promotori di salute e istruzione, miliziane e miliziani, insurgentes, responsabili organizzativi a livello locale, regionale, di zona e interzonale. Parte del tutto che costituisce la nuova direzione organizzativa zapatista.

Altri che, lottando, si sono conquistati un posto degno all’interno della comunità. E grazie a quel posto, si sono guadagnati rispetto e ammirazione.

Ragazze e ragazzi, dai 12 ai 20 anni, che sanno leggere e scrivere, utilizzano con disinvoltura tecnologie che i loro genitori non avrebbero nemmeno immaginato, che si avvicinano alle arti realizzando opere teatrali, film, dipinti, poesie, canzoni, balli, traducendo in quei linguaggi peculiari propri delle arti le loro vite, le loro storie, i loro sogni, i loro amori e le loro delusioni amorose, il loro retaggio, la loro lingua, la loro cultura, il loro essere comunità, con il cuore spezzato appena ieri, e oggi di nuovo sano e integro.

Bambine e bambini, il fatidico “Comando Palomitas”, il cui numero varia a seconda che ci siano o meno dolci al momento della ricreazione, l’infanzia di tutte le lingue, tutte uguali nel gioco e nelle marachelle, la risata infantile come vaccino contro tutte le frontiere umane.

Se guardiamo al calendario, ci sono cinque generazioni. Sei, se si conta quella che sta già arrivando e che si intravede nei ventri gonfi delle giovani madri. Tutte, tutti, todoas delle comunità indigene. Tutte, tutti, todoas con il sangue delle radici maya …

author: Administrador
title: FÜNF GENERATIONEN AUF DER SUCHE NACH JOSÉ MIGUEL (Antwort auf die Interviewanfragen)
content:
FÜNF GENERATIONEN AUF DER SUCHE NACH JOSÉ MIGUEL (Antwort auf die Interviewanfragen)

So heißt er: José Miguel. José Miguel Rodríguez Rodríguez. Er ist 29 Jahre alt und verschwand am 18. Juni 2026 in Salamanca, Guanajuato, zusammen mit Wendy Ángela Ruiz Luna und Brisa Johana Flores Luna. Das ist jetzt fast 6 Monate her.

Vor ein paar Tagen habe ich erzählt, wie SubMoisés in einem Vortrag vor der zapatistischen Delegation – als Teil ihrer Vorbereitung – darauf hinwies, dass das Wichtigste der Vermisste, die Vermisste sei. Also das Fehlen. Und er, SubMoy, betonte immer wieder, dass dieses Verschwinden wie eine Lücke, wie ein Loch, wie ein Biss im Leben der Angehörigen und Nahestehenden sei. Eine Leere, die nur durch die Anwesenheit der vermissten Person gefüllt werden könne, also durch das Auffinden des abwesenden Menschen.

Dass es kein Versprechen, kein politisches Geschwätz, kein Ermittlungsverfahren, keinen polizeilichen oder staatsanwaltlichen Einsatz, keine Demonstration, keine Kundgebung, keine Anzeige, keine Zählung, kein Transparent, kein Plakat, keinen Gesang, keine Statistik und keinen Schrei gebe, die dieses Fehlen „vollständig machen“ könne.

Und dann tat er so, als wäre er die verschwundene Person selbst, die sprach, die sich an ihre Angehörigen, Freund:innen und Nahestehenden wandte. Was sagte er ihnen? Er versetzte sich so in die Lage der vermissten Person und merkte, dass etwas nicht stimmte. Dass dieser Mensch, genauso wie er seinen Angehörigen fehlte, ebenfalls seine Familie, seine Arbeit, sein Studium, seine Liebe, seine Freund:innen, also sein Leben vermisste. Auch ihm war ein Stück von sich selbst, von seinem Wesen, entrissen worden, und da war eine ebenso große, ebenso schmerzhafte, ebenso quälende Lücke zurückgeblieben.

Und dass dieser Mensch ihnen zurief, dass er da sei, hinter dieser Tür, hinter diesem Zaun, hinter dieser Grenze, in diesem Gefängnis. Und er verzweifelte, weil seine Stimme nicht weit reichte, im Lärm erstickte, sich in anderen Schreien verlor.

Aber genauso wie diejenigen, die diesen Menschen suchen, darauf hoffen, ihn zu finden, hofft der Mensch selbst darauf, gefunden zu werden. Das war und ist das Wichtigste. Vollständig werden. Und er sagte seinen Angehörigen, sie sollten Kraft und Mut fassen. Und sie sollten auch schreien. Sie, damit er sie hörte, er, damit man ihn fände.

1530 Männer, Frauen, Andere, Jungen, Mädchen aus bis zu fünf Generationen hörten schweigend zu. Da waren Männer und Frauen, die über 70 Jahre alt waren, Urgroßväter und Urgroßmütter, die meisten Veteranen und Veteraninnen des Aufstands von 1994 und des Untergrunds, in dem der Krieg gegen das Vergessen einst vorbereitet wurde.

Erwachsene über 50, die ebenfalls losgezogen waren, um gegen ein System, einen Staat, eine Regierung, eine Armee, eine Polizei, ein Justizsystem, die Geschichte und das Schicksal zu kämpfen, sich gegen sie zu widersetzen und sie herauszufordern mit der Jugend und der Wut, die Vergessensein auslöst.

Väter und Mütter, verheiratet und ledig, zwischen 30 und 40 Jahren, die im Widerstand und in der Rebellion aufgewachsen sind und gelernt haben, dass sie – wenn sie sich organisieren – in Würde leben können. Sie sind autonome Autoritäten, Gesundheits- und Bildungspromotor:innen, Milizionäre und Milizionärinnen, Aufständische oder leiten die lokale, regionale, zonale und interzonale Organisation. Ein Teil des Ganzen, das die neue zapatistische Organisationsführung ausmacht.

Andere, die im Kampf einen würdigen Platz in der Gemeinschaft gefunden haben. Und sich mit diesem Platz Respekt und Bewunderung verschafft haben.

Jugendliche zwischen 12 und 20 Jahren, die lesen und schreiben können, die mühelos mit Technologien umgehen, von denen ihre Eltern nicht einmal zu träumen wagten, die in die Welt der Kunst eintauchen, indem sie Theaterstücke, Filme, Gemälde, Gedichte, Lieder und Tänze erschaffen und dabei ihr Leben, ihre Geschichten, ihre Träume, ihre Lieben und Enttäuschungen, ihr Erbe, ihre Sprache, ihre Kultur, ihr Gemeinschaftsgefühl in deren ganz eigene Sprachen übersetzen mit einem Herzen, das gestern noch gebrochen war, aber heute schon wieder gesund und ganz ist.

Mädchen und Jungen, das schicksalsträchtige „Comando Palomitas“, dessen Anzahl davon abhängt, ob es beim Durchzählen Süßigkeiten gibt oder nicht, die Kindheit aller Sprachen, die sich im Spiel und im Unfug einander angleichen, das kindliche Lachen als Impfstoff gegen alle menschlichen Grenzen.

Wenn wir uns den Kalender …

author: Randi Beers
title: News Quiz Nov. 14 | What day is it?
content:
It’s time again for a news quiz. Come on in and test your knowledge of current events.


1.

Silu’s Taxi in Rankin Inlet recently announced it would no longer operate. Aside from giving rides, what charitable activity did the company help with?


A.

 It operated as a medical transport service for patients flying south for health-care appointments.


B.

 The company hosted mechanic workshops to teach students the trade when its vehicles needed repair.


C.

 The company helped facilitate pizza deliveries to Leo Ussak Elementary School to celebrate the last day of classes.


2.

 What did Kuujjuaq commemorate this week with its Path to 100 festival?


A.

 Remembrance Day


B.

 The anniversary of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement


C.

 One-hundred years of Winnie the Pooh


3.

 What did people come together to celebrate Saturday at Annie Pootogook Park in Ottawa?


A.

 International Inuit Day


B.

 Bison Day


C.

 National Bittersweet Chocolate with Almonds Day


4

. Critics of the way Nunavut handles foster care point to an Indigenous-led method of family services that has worked for decades in which jurisdiction?


A.

 Alaska


B.

 Hawaii


C.

 Puerto Rico


5.

 Northern store’s security guards in Iqaluit look a little different these days. What has changed?


A.

 They dress for holidays throughout the year in an effort to spread cheer.


B.

 They are in tactical gear, including body cameras and carry what appear to be retractable batons.


C.

 The store is employing robot security guards now.


What are these two celebrating Saturday at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa? (File photo by Nehaa Bimal)


Answers:


1.

 C — Silu’s Taxi did more than offer rides for money. The company also

partnered

 with Slap Shot Canteen to deliver pizzas to Leo Ussak School to celebrate the final day of classes.


2.

 B — The festival, hosted in Kuujjuaq from Sunday to Wednesday,

commemorates

 the anniversary of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement by using art to imagine a path forward.


3.

 A — This one should be a gimme. People

gathered

 at Annie Pootoogook Park to celebrate National Inuit Day with sealskin tents, music and traditional food. Bison Day and National Bittersweet Chocolate with Almonds Day are apparently real, though. Nov. 7 was also Little League Girls Day, National Learn to Homebrew Day and National Canine Lymphoma Awareness Day.


4.

 B — Women’s advocate Arlene Hache told Nunatsiaq News she was

invited to share

 information about Hawaii’s community-based approach to foster care. “It wasn’t like it was radical or new,” Hache said of the idea. “But everything in the North is radical and new if it’s not colonial.” For now, the Department of Family Services isn’t looking to reinvent the wheel. It’s focusing on getting its staff trained on its online information management system.


5.

 B — Some of Northern store’s guards are now

geared up

 with tactical vests, body cameras and what appear to be batons. Nunatsiaq News asked about the batons but a manager with Canadian Arctic Protective Services declined to comment.

title: صد سال پس از انتشار    ویراست فرانسوی 1875–1872.کاپیتال  ِ   «ناشناخته »ی  ِ  مارکس:جلد  اول
content: در نتیجه، همچنان با ترجمه‌ای ناقص از جلد اول کاپیتال به زبان انگلیسی روبه‌رو هستیم. معنای این امر آن است که صفحات کاملی از برخی بخش‌های کتاب، از جمله بخش‌هایی از فصل «قانون عام انباشت سرمایه‌دارانه»، از متن حذف شده‌اند. افزون بر این، در موارد متعددی، متن فرانسوی مارکس حاوی جمله‌ها یا بندهایی با شکل‌بندی‌های جایگزین است که در ویراست‌های آلمانی، مطالب متناظر با آن‌ها به شکل دیگری آمده‌اند. در بسیاری از موارد، به نظر می‌رسد این شکل‌بندی‌های جایگزین، متأخرتر و از نظر بیان و پرداخت، پخته‌تر باشند؛ اما در هر حال، ما از امکان مقایسۀ این شکل‌بندی‌ها محروم مانده‌ایم.
